pages.title: Nmap — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: find every reachable service on a host, identify it precisely, prove what you found, and save the evidence — in that order.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core = run it almost always · Conditional = when a finding justifies it · Advanced = specialised, do not let it displace core enumeration. **Status:** Syntax Checked = flags verified against `nmap --help` and the installed script set (Nmap 7.99) · Documented — Untested = not executed against a live host here.

items: **Runs on:** Kali Linux.
**Needs:** `sudo` for SYN, UDP and OS scans; a route to `<TARGET_IP>`; confirmed scope.
**Output convention:** write every scan into `<OUTPUT_DIR>` (`./recon/<TARGET_IP>/`).

blocks.title: Confirm connectivity before blaming the target

commands.code: ip a; ip route get <TARGET_IP>; ping -c 3 <TARGET_IP>

fields.lookFor: `tun0` with an IP, a route whose `dev` is that interface, ICMP replies.
fields.decision: no route → reconnect the VPN. Route present but no reply → continue; most exam targets drop ICMP.
fields.mistake: scanning your own VPN subnet, or an IP left over from the previous box.
fields.evidence: note the confirmed IP in the machine notes.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** separate "target is down" from "my tunnel is broken".

blocks.title: Create the output directory

fields.lookFor: no output = success.
fields.decision: if the directory exists, reuse it — never delete earlier scans.
fields.mistake: scanning from `~` and losing the files among other boxes' output.
fields.evidence: the directory becomes part of the report trail.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** every scan lands somewhere predictable and survives the box.

blocks.title: Ping sweep

fields.lookFor: `Nmap scan report for ` per live host.
fields.decision: a host missing here may still be up (ICMP filtered). For a single known target, skip straight to Step 04 with `-Pn`.
fields.mistake: treating `-sn` as a port scan — it sends no TCP or UDP port probes, so it cannot find services.
fields.evidence: the host list, if you are enumerating a subnet.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** find live hosts in a range without probing ports.

blocks.text: **Why two scans?** The default scan covers the 1,000 most common ports and finishes in seconds-to-minutes — it is the fast first look. A 65,535-port scan finds services on high ports (8080, 8443, 5985, 49152+) that the default list never touches. Run the fast scan first so you have something to work with, then the full scan to close the gap.

blocks.title: Initial TCP scan (top 1,000)

fields.lookFor: `open` lines, and any filtered ports with a reason.
fields.decision: open ports → Step 06. All 1,000 filtered → Step 05 with `-Pn`, then review filtering.
fields.next: Step 05 (full range) — do not stop at the top 1,000.
fields.mistake: presenting the top-1,000 result as "all ports" and missing the second web app on 8081.
fields.evidence: the normal-format file.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** quick baseline of the ports most likely to matter.

blocks.title: Full TCP port discovery

fields.lookFor: any `open` port not present in Step 04 — these are usually the interesting ones.
fields.decision: if the scan finishes suspiciously fast or reports `host seems down`, drop `--min-rate` and retry with `-T3`. False negatives are worse than a slow scan.
fields.next: Step 06 on the complete open-port list.
fields.mistake: `--min-rate 5000` on a lossy link drops packets → missed ports. Lower the rate before trusting an empty result.
fields.evidence: keep the `.nmap`, `.gnmap` and `.xml` from `-oA`.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** find every listening TCP service.

blocks.title: Targeted version and script scan

fields.lookFor: `VERSION` column (product, version, extra info, OS hints) plus default-script output: titles, hostnames, certificates, share names.
fields.decision: version known → search for matching CVEs and move to Step 13-18 for the service's NSE scripts. Version hidden (`tcpwrapped`) → try `--version-all` (Step 08).
fields.next: Step 07 if a port looks filtered; otherwise Step 08.
fields.mistake: running `-sC -p-` in one pass — it is extremely slow. Restrict scripts to discovered ports.
fields.evidence: the scan plus the port/service table you will paste into the report.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** identify the exact product/version on the ports you actually found.

blocks.title: Investigate a filtered or ambiguous port

fields.lookFor: the `REASON` column (`syn-ack`, `reset`, `no-response`).
fields.decision: `reset` = closed · `no-response` = filtered or heavily rate-limited · `syn-ack` = open.
fields.next: if filtered, test the same service on an alternate port or move on; do not loop.
fields.mistake: assuming "filtered" means "nothing is there" — a firewall may simply be dropping your probe.
fields.evidence: the reason table, if you later report a filtered service.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** distinguish filtered, closed and open-but-silent.

blocks.title: Heavier version detection

fields.lookFor: a fuller `VERSION` string, sometimes with build numbers.
fields.decision: still nothing → banner-grab manually (`nc`) or use the service's own client.
fields.next: Step 13 for the relevant service family.
fields.mistake: expecting `-sV` to identify vulnerabilities. It reports a version banner; it does **not** prove a service is vulnerable.
fields.evidence: the version string you will match against exploit databases.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** squeeze a version out of a service that returned little.

blocks.title: Default scripts without version detection

fields.lookFor: titles, headers, certificate subjects, share and user listings.
fields.decision: a script error usually means the service is not what the port suggested — confirm with Step 06.
fields.mistake: `-sC` includes `http-title` etc. but is not a vulnerability scan.
fields.evidence: any hostname or username revealed here — it feeds DNS and vhost work.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** get script output quickly when you already know the version.

blocks.title: Top UDP ports

fields.lookFor: `open` or `open|filtered`.
fields.decision: `open|filtered` is normal and ambiguous — confirm with the service's own client (`dig`, `snmpwalk`) rather than rescanning.
fields.next: Step 11 for a suspected service, then its tool page.
fields.mistake: scanning all 65,535 UDP ports on the exam clock. It takes hours.
fields.evidence: the UDP table; note which ports were confirmed by a real client.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** catch services that only speak UDP (DNS 53, SNMP 161, NTP 123, IPMI 623, TFTP 69).

blocks.title: Targeted UDP with a script

fields.lookFor: a script response — that alone proves the port is open.
fields.decision: no response → treat as filtered and move on.
fields.next: SNMP → SNMP page · IPMI → note the firmware version.
fields.mistake: mixing UDP and TCP ports in one `-p` list without `-sU`; nmap scans them as TCP.
fields.evidence: the script output block.

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** confirm and fingerprint one UDP service.

blocks.title: OS fingerprint

fields.lookFor: `OS details:` or `Aggressive OS guesses:`.
fields.decision: one clean match → trust it enough to pick tools. No match → use service banners and TTL instead.
fields.next: choose the matching privilege-escalation page later.
fields.mistake: reading a single "Linux 4.x" guess as fact — VMs and firewalls routinely mislead it.
fields.evidence: the OS guess plus the evidence you actually relied on (banner, TTL).

blocks.notes: **Purpose:** decide between Linux and Windows tooling early.

fields.lookFor: page title, `Server:` header, allowed methods (`PUT` is interesting), enumerated paths, robots entries.
fields.decision: paths found → fetch them manually. `PUT` allowed → note it as a lead, do not upload yet.
fields.next: HTTP & HTTPS — Complete Command Reference for the full web workflow.
fields.mistake: `http-enum` is noisy and slow against large apps; it is a lead generator, not a directory brute-forcer.
fields.evidence: titles and paths; they are often the fastest route into the app.

fields.lookFor: hostname/domain/OS, `signing: enabled|disabled`, share names, account names.
fields.decision: shares listed → go to SMB — Complete Command Reference. Signing disabled → relay becomes worth investigating (prerequisites still apply).
fields.mistake: reading "signing disabled" as "relay will work". You still need a coercible authentication and a target that accepts the relayed identity.
fields.evidence: the OS/domain block — it is often the first proof you are facing a domain-joined host.

fields.lookFor: `Anonymous FTP login allowed`, server type/features, backdoor response.
fields.decision: anonymous allowed → FTP — Complete Command Reference Step 06. Backdoor script positive → validate manually before any exploit.
fields.mistake: firing a vsftpd exploit because the version is 2.3.4 — most 2.3.4 builds are not the backdoored one.
fields.evidence: the version banner and the anonymous result.

fields.lookFor: `zone-transfer:` records, or a transfer refusal.
fields.decision: transfer succeeds → every hostname goes into `/etc/hosts` and gets probed. Refused → normal; brute-force instead.
fields.mistake: running `dns-zone-transfer` without `--script-args` — the script has no domain to ask for.
fields.evidence: the full zone dump, if you get one.

fields.lookFor: accepted auth methods; weak KEX/ciphers/host-key algorithms.
fields.decision: `publickey` only + a key found on disk = worth trying. Password allowed → one careful attempt, not a brute force.
fields.mistake: treating weak algorithms as an authentication bypass. They are not.
fields.evidence: the auth-method line, before you attempt a login.

fields.lookFor: protocol version, auth salt, instance name, NTLM domain/host info.
fields.decision: MSSQL info leaks a domain name → useful for AD enumeration even before credentials.
fields.mistake: `ms-sql-ntlm-info` needs the instance to answer pre-auth; silence is not a closed port.
fields.evidence: instance and domain strings.

fields.lookFor: `VULNERABLE` blocks with CVE references.
fields.decision: every hit is a lead, not a finding — reproduce manually before reporting or exploiting.
fields.mistake: running this against fragile services on the exam; some scripts can crash a daemon and cost you the box.
fields.evidence: the CVE IDs, with the manual reproduction that confirmed them.

fields.lookFor: a script name matching the service in front of you.
fields.decision: no script → read the service's own documentation; NSE coverage is not exhaustive.
fields.mistake: guessing a script name. `--script-help` and the directory listing are authoritative.
fields.evidence: the exact script name you used, so the scan is reproducible.

fields.lookFor: three files appear: `.nmap` (readable), `.gnmap` (grep-able), `.xml` (machine-readable).
fields.decision: use `.gnmap` for quick greps (`grep open *.gnmap`), `.xml` for reporting tools.
fields.next: Step 22 if you want an HTML appendix.
fields.mistake: using `-oN` everywhere and later having to re-scan for structured data.
fields.evidence: all three files belong in `<OUTPUT_DIR>`.

blocks.title: Turn XML into an HTML appendix

fields.lookFor: a readable HTML file with the port table.
fields.decision: useful for the report appendix; not required for scoring.
fields.next: attach or reference it in the report notes.
fields.mistake: passing the `.nmap` file instead of the `.xml`.
fields.evidence: the HTML file plus the original XML.

blocks.title: Tune a slow or lossy scan

fields.lookFor: fewer `no-response` ports and a stable completion.
fields.decision: still missing ports → scan in ranges (`-p 1-10000`, `-p 10001-20000`) so a failure is contained.
fields.mistake: raising `-T` to compensate for packet loss. It makes loss worse.
fields.evidence: the timing options used — they explain why two scans differ.

blocks.title: Why aggressive timing lies
blocks.notes:
**Purpose:** decide when speed is safe.
- `-T4` is a reasonable default on a lab VPN.
- `-T5` and very high `--min-rate` values cause dropped probes and **false negatives**.
- `--max-retries 0` turns every lost packet into a missing port.
- Fragmentation (`-f`), decoys (`-D`) and spoofed source ports are **conditional** — they exist to test filtering, not to be defaults, and `-D` produces false positives in host lists.

blocks.title: Scan an internal host through SOCKS

fields.lookFor: a result at all — proxied scans are slow and lossy.
fields.decision: timeout → raise the proxy timeout and scan a single port; a whole-range scan through SOCKS is rarely worth it.
fields.next: once the port list is known, use the service's own client through the proxy.
fields.mistake: `-sS` through proxychains — SYN scans cannot traverse a SOCKS proxy; you must use `-sT`.
fields.evidence: note that the result came via proxy; the report should say so. > **Pivoting variant (all pages):** if you are targeting an internal host, prepend `proxychains4` and add `-Pn` to skip host discovery, which usually fails through a proxy.

blocks.text: | State | Meaning | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | `open` | A service accepted the connection | Enumerate it | | `closed` | Host replied with RST; nothing listening | No further action | | `filtered` | No reply — firewall dropped it | Try `--reason`, alternate ports, or move on | | `open\|filtered` | Cannot tell (UDP, or a firewall that eats RSTs) | Confirm with the service's own client |

items: **Version strings** are banners, not vulnerability proof. `Apache httpd 2.4.49` tells you which CVEs to research; it does not tell you the path is exploitable.
**TTL** near 64 suggests Linux/Unix, near 128 suggests Windows — a hint for tool selection, never a finding.
A single `open` port on a host with everything else filtered is a strong signal: it is probably the intended path.

blocks.text: | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `Host seems down` | ICMP blocked | Add `-Pn` | | All ports filtered | Host firewall, or wrong IP | Verify with `ip route get`; try a known-open port | | Scan hangs on one port | Service accepts but never replies | `--host-timeout`, or scan that port with `nc -w 3` | | Missing ports found by another tool | Rate too high / packet loss | Drop `--min-rate`, use `-T3`, retry the port | | `Failed to resolve` | Hostname not in DNS or `/etc/hosts` | Use the IP, or add the entry | | `QUITTING!` early | Interface changed mid-scan | Confirm VPN stability, rerun |
**Stop condition:** if two different scan strategies agree on the port list, stop scanning and start enumerating. Re-scanning the same host with the same options does not produce new information.

items: `ip a; ip route get <TARGET_IP>` — prove connectivity.
`mkdir -p <OUTPUT_DIR>` — set the evidence path.
`nmap -sn` — only when sweeping a subnet.
`sudo nmap -sS -T4 -oN...` — fast baseline.
`sudo nmap -p- --min-rate 5000 -T4 -oA...` — complete port list.
`sudo nmap -sCV -p <TARGET_PORT> -oA...` — identify what is open.
UDP top-50 — if the host looks sparse or a UDP service is suspected.
Service NSE — Steps 13-18 for every service you found.
Save `.nmap`/`.gnmap`/`.xml`, then open the matching tool page.
The three output files from `-oA` (do not overwrite them on a retry — use a new name).
The command line itself, including timing options.
Any hostname, domain, share or username revealed by NSE — these are credentials-adjacent.
A screenshot of the port table if the report requires visual proof.
Nmap reference guide: [https://nmap.org/book/man.html](https://nmap.org/book/man.html)
NSE script documentation: [https://nmap.org/nsedoc/](https://nmap.org/nsedoc/)
Port scanning techniques: [https://nmap.org/book/man-port-scanning-techniques.html](https://nmap.org/book/man-port-scanning-techniques.html)

blocks.text: Every flag on this page was checked against `nmap --help` and the installed script directory on **Nmap 7.99**. No scan here was run against a live target, so all statuses are **Syntax Checked** or **Documented — Untested**, never **Lab Tested**. Behaviour that depends on the target (filtering, timing, IPv6) can only be confirmed during real enumeration.

pages.title: SMB — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: take SMB from "port 445 is open" to "I have read every share this account can reach, and I know whether signing matters" — on one page.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core / Conditional / Advanced. **Status:** Syntax Checked = checked against `smbclient`, `smbmap` and `nxc` help on this machine · Documented — Untested = not executed against a live host.

items: **Runs on:** Kali Linux.
**Needs:** `smbclient`, `smbmap`, `nxc` (all installed here); `impacket-smbclient` for the Impacket variant.
**Scope note:** null/guest sessions and share browsing are enumeration. Writing, deleting or relaying is **not** — confirm it is authorised first.

blocks.text: If the target is reachable only through a pivot, prepend `proxychains4` and keep the rest unchanged: `proxychains4 nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> --shares`. `smbclient` and `rpcclient` also traverse a SOCKS proxy, but every file download goes through it — copy single files instead of mirroring. If SMB stalls through SOCKS, forward the port instead: `ssh -L 4455:<TARGET_IP>:445 <USERNAME>@<PIVOT_HOST>`, then `smbclient -p 4455 -L //127.0.0.1/`.

blocks.title: Confirm SMB and grab the version

fields.lookFor: `microsoft-ds` on 445, `netbios-ssn` on 139, and a `VERSION` string with the host/domain.
fields.decision: open → Step 02. 445 closed but 139 open → older stack; still worth enumerating.
fields.mistake: stopping at "445 open" without a version — the version decides whether SMBv1 or a known CVE is even relevant.
fields.evidence: the port table and version string.

fields.lookFor: hostname, domain, OS build, `message_signing` state, share list, account list.
fields.decision: shares listed → Step 05. `signing: disabled` → read section I before acting on it.
fields.mistake: `smb-enum-users` needs a null session; an empty result usually means null sessions are off, not that there are no users.
fields.evidence: the OS/domain block and the share list.

blocks.title: Read the dialect and signing requirements

fields.lookFor: `SMB2/3 message signing enabled but not required` vs `required`.
fields.decision: "enabled but not required" = signing is optional → relay is *possible* in principle. "required" → relay to this host will fail.
fields.mistake: equating "signing not required" with "relay will work". Feasibility still depends on a coerced authentication and on the relayed identity having access.
fields.evidence: the exact signing line — quote it in the report.

blocks.title: Force a protocol version when negotiation fails

fields.lookFor: a share listing instead of `protocol negotiation failed`.
fields.decision: SMB1-only host → `-m NT1` (lab only; SMB1 is a red flag worth reporting).
fields.mistake: assuming a negotiation failure means the host is unreachable — it usually means the dialect is mismatched.
fields.evidence: the dialect you had to force.

fields.lookFor: a `Sharename Type Comment` table including `IPC$`, `C$`, `ADMIN$`.
fields.decision: `NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` → null sessions are disabled: move to credentialed enumeration. Listing works → Step 06.
fields.mistake: `-L` is the list flag and is case-sensitive; `-l` does not exist.
fields.evidence: the share table.

fields.lookFor: a `Disk`/`Permissions` table with `READ ONLY`, `READ, WRITE`, or `NO ACCESS`.
fields.decision: any `READ` → Step 08. `READ, WRITE` → note it; uploading is a separate, authorised decision.
fields.mistake: empty `-u ''` is a null attempt, not a guest login — try both. `NO ACCESS` on `C$` for a low-priv account is normal.
fields.evidence: the per-share permission table.

fields.lookFor: `SMB` banner with host/domain, then share lines with `READ`/`WRITE`.
fields.decision: `[+]` with guest → same path as Step 06. `STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` → no anonymous access.
fields.mistake: NetExec is noisy in logs; it is fine in a lab, but it is not a stealth tool.
fields.evidence: the banner is a quick source of hostname/domain strings.

fields.lookFor: an indented tree — backup folders, `IT`, `Finance`, user home directories, `*.bak`, `*.config`, scripts.
fields.decision: a directory looks interesting → Step 09 to pull it, or Step 11 to grab one file.
fields.mistake: **capital ****`-R`**** is not a valid smbmap flag.** The recursive flag is lowercase `-r`. `-R` fails with `unrecognized arguments: -R` (verified with `smbmap -h`; some course material prints it in uppercase).
fields.evidence: the tree, saved with `-g` if you want a grep-able output file.

fields.lookFor: file names, sizes, dates; recently modified files are usually the intended lead.
fields.decision: readable files → Step 10 or 11. `NO ACCESS` on a subdirectory → try the parent or another account.
fields.mistake: quoting the path — spaces in share or directory names break the argument without single quotes.
fields.evidence: the listing with timestamps.

fields.lookFor: `smb: \>` prompt, or `NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` / `NT_STATUS_BAD_NETWORK_NAME`.
fields.decision: prompt appears → `ls`, `cd`, `recurse ON`, `prompt OFF`, `mget *`. Access denied → wrong account or wrong share name (case-insensitive but must exist).
fields.mistake: using `//<TARGET_IP>\<SHARE_NAME>` — smbclient wants forward slashes in the UNC path.
fields.evidence: a transcript of the listing you relied on.

commands.code:
mkdir -p <OUTPUT_DIR> && cd <OUTPUT_DIR>
smbclient -N //<TARGET_IP>/<SHARE_NAME> -c 'recurse ON; prompt OFF; mget *'

fields.lookFor: `getting file \path\file` lines, then files on disk.
fields.decision: transfer errors on long paths → download subdirectories one at a time with `cd`/`mget`.
fields.mistake: running it from your home directory — you lose track of which box the files came from. Run inside `<OUTPUT_DIR>`.
fields.evidence: the mirrored tree itself.

fields.lookFor: the file appearing locally at the target path, or a `file not found` error.
fields.decision: success → Step 13. Failure on a path that was listed → quote the path exactly; spaces need quoting.
fields.mistake: downloading to a name that already exists — you silently overwrite earlier evidence.
fields.evidence: the file plus its source path.

fields.lookFor: config files, `.kdbx`, `.pfx`, scripts with hardcoded credentials, database backups, `unattend.xml`, `.ssh` directories.
fields.decision: credentials found → validate them carefully (Step 14) and record where they came from. Nothing found → continue enumeration; not every share is the path.
fields.mistake: grepping only for "password" — also try `pw`, `sa`, `uid=`, `user id=`, and base64-looking strings.
fields.evidence: the file path plus the exact line containing the credential.

blocks.title: Validate credentials and enumerate the domain in one pass

fields.lookFor: `[+]` auth success, share permissions, user list with `badpwdcount`, group memberships, active sessions, lockout policy.
fields.decision: `(Pwn3d!)` → local admin, move to secrets dumping (Advanced). Valid but no admin → harvest more shares and BloodHound data.
fields.mistake: running `--users` before reading `--pass-pol` — you may be two attempts from locking out every account.
fields.evidence: the auth line (host + domain + user), the share table, the policy.

blocks.title: Re-enumerate every share with the new identity

fields.lookFor: shares that were `NO ACCESS` before and are now readable — this is the single most common "new credential" win.
fields.decision: new access → back to Step 09/11 with that share.
fields.mistake: assuming your first enumeration was complete. Permissions are per-account; every new credential means re-running the basics.
fields.evidence: the before/after permission difference.

fields.lookFor: `user:[name] rid:[0x...]`, group lists, domain info.
fields.decision: users found → build a username list (never brute force before reading the password policy).
fields.mistake: RID cycling (`impacket-lookupsid`) is noisy and often unnecessary once you have one credential.
fields.evidence: the user/group list with RIDs.

blocks.title: Follow usernames
blocks.notes:
- Collect every `sAMAccountName` into `<USERLIST>`.
- Check the password policy before any spraying (`--pass-pol`).
- Reuse found credentials across SMB, WinRM, RDP and MSSQL — one password often opens two services.
- A username with no password is still useful: it feeds Kerberos user enumeration and AS-REP roasting.

blocks.title: Follow files and backups
blocks.notes:
- `*.bak`, `*.old`, `*.zip`, `*.7z`, `*.vhd`, `*.kdbx` → extract and grep.
- PowerShell scripts and `.bat` files often contain service-account credentials.
- `web.config`/`appsettings.json` → connection strings with SQL credentials.
- `unattend.xml`, `sysprep.inf` → local admin passwords (sometimes base64).

blocks.title: Follow configuration and scripts
blocks.notes:
- A script that maps a drive or calls `net use` reveals credentials and share names.
- A scheduled task definition reveals a service account.
- Note the file path: it is evidence and often the answer to "where did this credential come from?".

sections.title: Signing, relay feasibility and prerequisites
sections.rawTitle: H. Signing, relay feasibility and prerequisites

fields.lookFor: hosts where signing is not required, one IP per line.
fields.decision: domain controllers never appear (they require signing). A non-empty list is a *candidate* list, nothing more.
fields.mistake: treating this output as proof of exploitability. Relay needs (1) a host that does not require signing, (2) a coerced or captured authentication, (3) an identity with access to the target.
fields.evidence: the candidate list plus the signing evidence from Step 03.

fields.lookFor: `VULNERABLE` with the CVE-2017-0143 family.
fields.decision: vulnerable → confirm patch level and prerequisites before any attempt; this exploit can crash the host.
fields.next: validate in a snapshot if the exam allows it.
fields.mistake: running EternalBlue against a fragile exam VM and losing the box.
fields.evidence: the script output, and the OS build that supports the claim.

blocks.text: | Error | Meaning | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `NT_STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE` | Bad credentials, or wrong domain | Check `-d <DOMAIN>`; try `--local-auth` in NetExec | | `NT_STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` | Authenticated but no rights to that share | Try another share or account; check `smbmap` permissions | | `NT_STATUS_BAD_NETWORK_NAME` | Share name does not exist | Re-list shares; watch spaces and `$` suffixes | | `NT_STATUS_IO_TIMEOUT` | 445 filtered | Try 139 (`-p 139`), or confirm the host is up | | `protocol negotiation failed` | Dialect mismatch | `-m SMB2` / `-m SMB3` / `-m NT1` | | `session setup failed: NT_STATUS_MORE_PROCESSING_REQUIRED` | Kerberos clock skew or unsupported auth | Sync time (`sudo ntpdate <DC>` / `timedatectl`), or use NTLM | | `smbclient: command not found` | Package missing | `sudo apt install smbclient smbmap` | | Works with IP, fails with hostname | Name resolution | Add the entry to `/etc/hosts` |
**Stop condition:** if null, guest and one credential all fail and the share list is empty, SMB is probably not the entry point — move to another service and come back only with a new credential.

items: `nmap -sCV -p139,445` — confirm and version.
NSE baseline (Step 02) — OS, domain, shares, users.
`smbclient -N -L //<TARGET_IP>/` — null session.
`smbmap -H <TARGET_IP> -u '' -p ''` — permissions.
`smbmap -r <SHARE_NAME> --dir-only` — map the tree (lowercase `-r`).
Download and inspect (Steps 11-13).
With credentials: `nxc smb... --shares --users --groups --pass-pol`.
Re-run Steps 5-6 with the new identity.
Record signing status and whether relay is *actually* feasible.
The port/version table and the SMB signing line.
The share table **before and after** each new credential.
File paths (not just contents) of anything containing credentials.
The exact command used to retrieve each file, so the path is reproducible.
Samba `smbclient` manual: [https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smbclient.1.html](https://www.samba.org/samba/docs/current/man-html/smbclient.1.html)
smbmap usage: [https://github.com/ShawnDEvans/smbmap](https://github.com/ShawnDEvans/smbmap)
NetExec wiki: [https://www.netexec.wiki/](https://www.netexec.wiki/)
MS17-010 advisory: [https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2017/ms17-010](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securitybulletins/2017/ms17-010)

blocks.text: Flags were checked against `smbclient --help`, `smbmap -h` and `nxc smb --help` on this machine. The `smbmap -R` defect was reproduced (`unrecognized arguments: -R x`), which is why this page uses lowercase `-r` throughout. No SMB session was opened against a live host for this page, so nothing here is **Lab Tested**.

pages.title: FTP — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: confirm FTP, test anonymous access, pull everything readable, and know exactly what to check next — without confusing FTP, FTPS and SFTP.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core / Conditional / Advanced. **Status:** Syntax Checked (flags checked locally) · Documented — Untested (not run against a live host).

items: **Runs on:** Kali Linux.
**Needs:** `ftp` or `lftp`; `wget`/`curl`; `nmap`.
**Protocol distinction — do not mix these up:**
**FTP** — port 21 control, plaintext, separate data connection (active/passive).
**FTPS** — FTP over TLS; still port 21 with `AUTH TLS`, or implicit on 990.
**SFTP** — SSH subsystem on port 22. It is **not** FTP and none of the FTP commands below apply. Use SSH — Complete Command Reference.

blocks.text: `proxychains4 ftp -p <TARGET_IP>` carries the control channel, but FTP needs a **second** data connection, which SOCKS handles badly. Prefer an explicit forward: `ssh -L 2121:<TARGET_IP>:21 <USERNAME>@<PIVOT_HOST>`, then `ftp -p 127.0.0.1 2121` (passive). If active mode is required, the forward must be reversed — `ssh -R` — because the target connects back to you.

fields.lookFor: `21/tcp open ftp` plus product/version, and whether `ftp-syst`/`ftp-anon` ran as part of `-sC`.
fields.decision: open → Step 02. Version like `vsftpd 3.0.3` is common and **not** automatically vulnerable.
fields.mistake: assuming the banner version is exploitable — check the distribution's patches first.
fields.evidence: the banner and version.

fields.lookFor: `Anonymous FTP login allowed`, `ftp-syst` server type/features, backdoor response.
fields.decision: anonymous allowed → Step 03. Backdoor positive → Step 09 (validate first; most 2.3.4 builds are clean).
fields.mistake: `ftp-bounce` is obsolete on modern servers; a positive result still needs manual confirmation.
fields.evidence: the anonymous result — it is usually the whole path.

fields.lookFor: `220 (vsFTPd 3.0.3)` or similar; sometimes a hostname or internal domain.
fields.decision: banner reveals a hostname → add it to `/etc/hosts` and check DNS/vhosts.
fields.mistake: leaving the connection open — type `QUIT` or Ctrl-C.
fields.evidence: the banner line, especially any hostname.

fields.lookFor: `230 Login successful` (or `230 Anonymous access granted`).
fields.decision: success → Step 06. `530` → anonymous disabled, move on unless you have credentials.
fields.mistake: `-p` means **passive mode**, not "port". The login is `anonymous` with any password (conventionally an email).
fields.evidence: the login response and directory listing.

fields.lookFor: `lftp:~>` prompt.
fields.decision: works → `ls`, then `mirror` (Step 07). Fails → fall back to `ftp` or `wget`.
fields.mistake: lftp is not always installed (`sudo apt install lftp`); it is optional.
fields.evidence: same as Step 04.

commands.code:
ftp -p <TARGET_IP>
# at the ftp> prompt
ls -la
binary

fields.lookFor: directories named `backup`, `public`, `upload`, `www`, `conf`; dotfiles; `*.zip`, `*.sql`, `*.bak`.
fields.decision: `www` or `public_html` present → the FTP root may be web-served: check HTTP & HTTPS — Complete Command Reference on 80/443.
fields.mistake: forgetting `binary` before downloading archives — ASCII mode corrupts zips and binaries.
fields.evidence: the recursive listing.

fields.lookFor: a mirrored tree and a transfer log ending without errors.
fields.decision: passive mode fails (`425`) → add `--no-passive-ftp` (forces active; only if your host is reachable from the target). Credentials → `ftp://<USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>@<TARGET_IP>/`.
fields.mistake: credentials in the URL end up in shell history and process listings — acceptable in a lab, not in real engagements.
fields.evidence: the mirrored files with timestamps.

blocks.title: Single file over an interactive session

commands.code:
ftp -p <TARGET_IP>
# at the ftp> prompt
binary
get <FILE> <OUTPUT_FILE>

fields.lookFor: `226 Transfer complete`.
fields.decision: `550 Failed to open file` → wrong path or no read permission.
fields.mistake: `get file` without an output path writes to the current directory and can overwrite evidence.
fields.evidence: the file and the exact command.

fields.lookFor: config files, SQL dumps, SSH keys, scripts with credentials, `.bash_history`, `*.bak`.
fields.decision: credentials → validate elsewhere (SSH/SMB/HTTP). Source code → look for upload endpoints and hardcoded paths.
fields.next: Step 10, or the service the credentials belong to.
fields.mistake: only reading filenames — the interesting data is usually inside `.conf`, `.env`, `*.sql`, `*.php`.
fields.evidence: file path plus the line containing the finding.

blocks.title: Check the version against known issues

fields.lookFor: matching exploits and their required conditions.
fields.decision: candidate found → read it fully and confirm the exact build before running anything.
fields.mistake: the vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor (CVE-2011-2523) only affects the specific trojanised source release — most distributions shipped a clean 2.3.4.
fields.evidence: the version string plus the exploit's prerequisites.

blocks.title: Test write permission with a harmless file

commands.code:
echo test > /tmp/test.txt
ftp -p <TARGET_IP>
# at the ftp> prompt
put /tmp/test.txt

fields.lookFor: `226 Transfer complete`, or `550 Permission denied`.
fields.decision: writable **and** the directory maps to a web root → an upload path may exist; confirm the web path before uploading anything else. Writable but not web-served → limited value.
fields.next: HTTP & HTTPS — Complete Command Reference if web-served.
fields.mistake: overwriting or deleting existing files. Upload a new, uniquely named file and remove it afterwards.
fields.evidence: the upload confirmation and the resulting URL/path.

blocks.title: Prerequisites before attempting anything
blocks.notes:
- **Backdoored vsftpd 2.3.4** — only the trojanised release; trigger opens a shell on 6200. Confirm the build first; this is not a generic 2.3.4 exploit.
- **Anonymous write + web root** — upload a webshell only if the FTP directory is served by HTTP and the extension is executable.
- **Weak credentials** — after reading any policy; FTP has no lockout by default, but brute force is slow and noisy.
- **ProFTPD ****`mod_copy`** — `SITE CPFR`/`SITE CPTO` can copy files without auth on misconfigured servers (version-dependent).
> Every item above is a lab technique. None of them is a first step, and each needs its precondition verified first.

blocks.text: | Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `530 Login incorrect` | Bad credentials, or anonymous disabled | Try `anonymous`/any password; verify the username | | `530 Permission denied` after login | Account lacks FTP rights | Try another account | | `425 Failed to establish connection` | Passive data port blocked | `passive` / `-p` on, or `--no-passive-ftp` in wget as a last resort | | Connection hangs after `230` | Data channel blocked | Switch passive/active mode | | `550 Failed to open file` | Path or permission | `ls` the exact directory first | | `AUTH TLS` refused | Plain FTP only | Use `ftp`, not FTPS | | `SSL_connect: wrong version` | FTPS server with a legacy TLS version | `openssl s_client -connect <TARGET_IP>:21 -starttls ftp` to inspect |
**Stop condition:** anonymous denied, no credentials, and no writable or web-served directory → FTP is a dead end. Move to the next service.

items: `nmap -sCV -p21` — version.
`nmap --script ftp-anon,ftp-syst,ftp-vsftpd-backdoor -p21` — anonymous check.
`ftp -p <TARGET_IP>` — log in as `anonymous`, `ls -la`.
`wget -m ftp://anonymous:anonymous@<TARGET_IP>/` — mirror.
`file` + `grep` the loot — credentials, configs, source.
`searchsploit

blocks.text: ` — only if the version is unusual.

items: Write test — only if authorised and the directory looks web-served.
Record the banner, the anonymous result, and every file path you used.
The `220` banner and the `230` anonymous response.
The recursive directory listing.
Every downloaded file, kept in `<OUTPUT_DIR>` with its original name.
The exact `get`/`wget` command for anything you quote in the report.
`ftp(1)` — `-p` is passive mode: [https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/ftp.1.html](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/ftp.1.html)
NSE `ftp-anon`: [https://nmap.org/nsedoc/scripts/ftp-anon.html](https://nmap.org/nsedoc/scripts/ftp-anon.html)
vsftpd security notes: [https://security.appspot.com/vsftpd.html](https://security.appspot.com/vsftpd.html)

No FTP session was opened against a live host for this page; everything is **Syntax Checked** or **Documented — Untested**. The `ftp -p` clarification (passive mode, not port) is a correction of a common misreading, not a lab result.

pages.title: DNS — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: turn an IP into names, records and (when you are lucky) a full zone — then hand those names to the web and AD pages.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core / Conditional / Advanced. **Status:** Syntax Checked · Documented — Untested.

items: **Runs on:** Kali Linux.
**Needs:** `dig` (bind9-dnsutils), `dnsenum`, `dnsrecon`; a wordlist for bruteforce.
**Always query the target's resolver** with `@<TARGET_IP>`. Without it you are asking your own DNS and learning nothing about the target.

blocks.text: SOCKS carries TCP only, so force TCP: `proxychains4 dig +tcp @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN>`. A plain UDP `dig` through proxychains will simply time out. Zone transfers are already TCP, so `proxychains4 dig axfr @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN>` works unchanged.

fields.lookFor: `domain` on 53/tcp, and a BIND/NSID response on UDP.
fields.decision: TCP 53 open is required for zone transfers; UDP is enough for ordinary queries.
fields.mistake: concluding "no DNS" from a UDP `open|filtered` result — confirm with `dig`.
fields.evidence: the version and whether TCP 53 is open.

fields.lookFor: one or more addresses. Empty output with `NOERROR` means the name exists but has no record of that type.
fields.decision: an internal IP resolves → add it to your target list and scan it.
fields.mistake: dropping `@<TARGET_IP>` and hitting your own resolver (or the internet).
fields.evidence: the resolved addresses.

commands.code:
dig @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN> NS +short
dig @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN> MX +short
dig @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN> TXT +short
dig @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN> CNAME +short
dig @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN> SOA +short

fields.lookFor: authoritative name servers, mail hosts, SPF/verification strings, the SOA's primary NS and admin mailbox.
fields.decision: NS names → resolve and test each for a zone transfer (Step 05). MX hosts → SMTP enumeration. SOA → the zone's primary server, often the DC.
fields.mistake: treating TXT as noise — SPF records leak internal hostnames and third-party services.
fields.evidence: the record set per type.

fields.lookFor: a hostname, or nothing.
fields.decision: name returned → resolve it forward and check for sibling hosts. Empty → normal.
fields.mistake: expecting PTRs for private ranges unless the DNS server is authoritative for them (common in AD labs).
fields.evidence: the name, if any.

fields.lookFor: a full record listing, or `Transfer failed`.
fields.decision: success → every hostname goes into `/etc/hosts` and gets probed (Step 07). Failure → normal, secure configuration; go to Step 06.
fields.next: Step 07 on success, Step 06 on failure.
fields.mistake: trying only one server. Repeat the AXFR against each NS from Step 03 — one may allow it while another refuses.
fields.evidence: the full zone dump, saved to `<OUTPUT_FILE>`.

fields.lookFor: host records, bruteforced names, and its own AXFR attempt.
fields.decision: new hostnames → resolve and probe them. Nothing → try Step 07 with a different wordlist.
fields.mistake: `--dnsserver` is mandatory for internal domains; without it dnsenum queries public DNS and returns nothing useful.
fields.evidence: the host list.

fields.lookFor: SRV records, A/NS/MX tables, bruteforced subdomains.
fields.decision: SRV records for `_ldap._tcp` / `_kerberos._tcp` → you have found a domain controller (Step 08).
fields.mistake: `-t std` is passive-ish and fast; `-t brt` needs a wordlist and time — do not run it blind against a huge list.
fields.evidence: the SRV block.

fields.lookFor: `getent` returning the target IP.
fields.decision: names resolve → browse by hostname and re-run vhost discovery.
fields.mistake: overwriting `/etc/hosts` instead of appending, and adding names you have not confirmed.
fields.evidence: the `/etc/hosts` line.

commands.code:
dig @<DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> _ldap._tcp.<DOMAIN> SRV +short
dig @<DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> _kerberos._tcp.<DOMAIN> SRV +short
dig @<DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP> _gc._tcp.<DOMAIN> SRV +short

fields.lookFor: `0 100 389..` style answers.
fields.decision: a DC hostname appears → add it to `/etc/hosts` and start AD enumeration.
fields.mistake: querying with the FQDN of the DC but not adding the record for `<DOMAIN>` itself — Kerberos needs both name forms.
fields.evidence: the SRV answers — they prove the domain name and the DC.

blocks.text: | Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `connection timed out; no servers could be reached` | UDP 53 filtered | `dig +tcp @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN>` | | `REFUSED` | Recursion disabled for your source | Query the authoritative zone directly; try AXFR | | `NXDOMAIN` | Name does not exist | Correct name, or brute-force | | `SERVFAIL` | Broken zone or forwarding | Try another NS | | `no servers could be reached` on `-x` | Private range not in DNS | Normal; use forward records instead | | AXFR `Transfer failed` | Transfers restricted | Try each NS; otherwise brute-force |
**Stop condition:** if A, NS and AXFR all fail, DNS is probably not the path. Move on and return only if a hostname appears elsewhere.

items: `nmap -sCV -p53` — confirm TCP/UDP DNS.
`dig @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN> A/NS/MX/TXT` — records.
`dig axfr @<TARGET_IP> <DOMAIN>` — transfers, then against each NS.
`dnsenum --dnsserver <TARGET_IP> -f <WORDLIST> <DOMAIN>` — brute force.
Add names to `/etc/hosts` and probe them.
In AD: query the SRV records, then move to the AD page.
The record dump per type.
Any zone transfer output, unedited.
The `/etc/hosts` entries you added (they explain later results).
The resolver you queried — results differ per server.
`dig` manual: [https://bind9.readthedocs.io/en/latest/manpages.html](https://bind9.readthedocs.io/en/latest/manpages.html)
DNS record types: [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035)
dnsrecon: [https://github.com/darkoperator/dnsrecon](https://github.com/darkoperator/dnsrecon)

blocks.text: Flags were checked against the local `dig`, `dnsenum` and `dnsrecon` help output. No query was sent to a live target for this page, so all statuses are **Syntax Checked** or **Documented — Untested**.

pages.title: HTTP & HTTPS — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: fingerprint the web app, map its surface, and know which request to send next — with passive checks separated from intrusive ones.

blocks.text: **Priority:** Core / Conditional / Advanced. **Status:** Syntax Checked = flags checked locally · Documented — Untested = standard tool, not run here · Version-Dependent = behaviour varies by release.

items: **Runs on:** Kali Linux.
**Needs:** `curl`, `whatweb`, `nikto`, `openssl`, `ffuf` (installed); `sslscan`, `testssl.sh`, `hakrawler`, `katana` (optional).
**Three tiers, keep them separate:**
**Passive fingerprinting** — headers, titles, certificates. Safe, low noise.
**Manual validation** — fetch a path, read the response. Still safe.
**Intrusive checks** — fuzzing, auth attempts, injection probes. Can lock accounts, trigger WAFs or crash the app. Only with authorisation.

blocks.text: `proxychains4 curl -i -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/` works for single requests. For anything stateful (sessions, Burp, a browser), forward the port instead: `ssh -L 8080:<TARGET_IP>:80 <USERNAME>@<PIVOT_HOST>` and browse `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` — that keeps cookies, redirects and Burp's proxy chain intact.

fields.lookFor: server banner, page title, allowed methods (`PUT`, `DELETE` are leads), redirects.
fields.decision: non-standard port or odd banner → Step 02. `PUT` allowed → note it, do not upload.
fields.mistake: scanning only 80/443. Repeat for every HTTP-ish port from the full scan (8080, 8000, 8443, 3000, 5000).
fields.evidence: the title/server pair for each port — they often differ per vhost.

fields.lookFor: CMS + version, framework, JS libraries, server, cookies set by the app.
fields.decision: a CMS with a version → search for matching plugins/CVEs. A custom app → go to Step 03 and manual review.
fields.mistake: `-a 3` is aggressive and detectable; start with `-a 1` and only escalate when you need more detail.
fields.evidence: the plugin/version list. **Old page content preserved:** the original `WhatWeb` note also used `whatweb --no-errors 192.168.1.0/24` (network sweep) and `whatweb -v`. Both are valid; the sweep form is only useful on a subnet you own.

commands.code:
curl -i -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/
curl -i -sS -L http://<TARGET_IP>/ -o <OUTPUT_FILE>
curl -I -sS https://<TARGET_IP>/ -k

fields.lookFor: `Server:`, `X-Powered-By:`, `Set-Cookie:`, `Location:`, security headers that are missing.
fields.decision: `Location:` to a hostname → add it to `/etc/hosts` and re-request. Cookie flags missing (`HttpOnly`, `Secure`) → note for later.
fields.mistake: `-I` sends HEAD; some apps behave differently than with GET. Use `-i` when the body matters.
fields.evidence: the full header block. **Old page content preserved:** the original `curl` note listed `curl -v`, `curl -X POST`, and `curl -IL`. All still valid: `-v` for the TLS/connection trace, `-X POST -d 'a=b'` for form posts, `-IL` for headers after redirects.

blocks.title: Compare codes and redirects across paths

commands.code:
for p in / /admin /login /api /robots.txt; do
 printf '%-12s ' "$p"; curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download} %{redirect_url}\n' "http://<TARGET_IP>$p"
done

fields.lookFor: 200 vs 301/302 vs 401/403 vs 404, and different response sizes.
fields.decision: 401/403 proves the path exists — worth deeper inspection. 302 to `/login` is normal for a protected app.
fields.mistake: treating every 200 as "found" — wildcard/catch-all apps return 200 for everything; compare body sizes.
fields.evidence: the code/size table.

commands.code:
curl -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/robots.txt
curl -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/sitemap.xml
curl -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/ | grep -Eo '(src|href)="[^"]+"' | sort -u

fields.lookFor: `Disallow:` paths, sitemap URLs, script/style references, comments in the HTML.
fields.decision: any listed path → request it directly. JS files → Step 08.
fields.mistake: checking robots only on the main host — each vhost has its own.
fields.evidence: the disallowed paths and any endpoint-looking URL.

fields.lookFor: CN, SANs, validity dates, internal issuer.
fields.decision: SANs contain hostnames you have not seen → add them to `/etc/hosts` and probe.
fields.mistake: omitting `-servername` — without SNI you get the default vhost's certificate and miss the rest.
fields.evidence: the SAN list — often the cheapest source of new hostnames. **Old page content preserved:** `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443` (the original note) is the same command without SNI or the certificate decode pipe.

fields.lookFor: protocol versions, weak ciphers, expired/self-signed certificates, known TLS CVEs.
fields.decision: legacy protocols enabled → note it as a hardening finding. It is rarely a direct path to a shell.
fields.mistake: reporting a TLS weakness as an exploitation finding — it is a configuration issue unless you can demonstrate impact.
fields.evidence: the protocol/cipher summary line.

fields.lookFor: a different body size or status per `Host` value.
fields.decision: a hit → add it to `/etc/hosts` and run Steps 01-05 against it as a new site.
fields.mistake: relying on status codes — many servers return 200 for unknown hosts. Filter by size, or use `-ac`.
fields.evidence: the vhost name and its size difference. > **Content discovery belongs on one page.** Wordlist-driven directory/file brute force (`feroxbuster`, `gobuster`, `ffuf` path mode) is documented in **Directory and Virtual Host Enumeration — Complete Command Reference** *(batch 5)*. This page covers the manual and fingerprinting side only, so the two never drift apart.

fields.lookFor: `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm=...` (HTTP Basic), a login form in the HTML (form/session), `Set-Cookie` after login.
fields.decision: Basic auth → credentials are sent in every request; try found credentials. Form login → capture the request in Burp and replay it.
fields.mistake: assuming a 401 means "no access" — it often confirms the path exists and tells you the realm name.
fields.evidence: the `WWW-Authenticate` header or the form's action/method.

commands.code:
curl -i -sS -c cookies.txt -d 'username=<USERNAME>&password=<PASSWORD>' http://<TARGET_IP>/login
curl -sS -b cookies.txt http://<TARGET_IP>/dashboard

fields.lookFor: a session cookie, then a successful authenticated page.
fields.decision: session works → browse the authenticated surface; it is usually where the vulnerability lives.
fields.mistake: guessing the form field names — copy them from the actual HTML or Burp.
fields.evidence: the request that authenticated and the response that proved it.

commands.code:
curl -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/ | grep -Eo 'src="[^"]+\.js[^"]*"' | sort -u
curl -sS http://<TARGET_IP>/js/app.js | grep -Eo '"/[a-zA-Z0-9_/.-]+"' | sort -u

fields.lookFor: API paths, hidden admin routes, API keys, feature flags.
fields.decision: endpoints found → request them (Step 04) and check for missing auth.
fields.mistake: only reading the visible page — SPAs put everything in the bundle.
fields.evidence: the endpoint list with the file it came from.

fields.lookFor: URLs, parameters, forms, JS files.
fields.decision: new endpoints → Step 04. Nothing new → the app is small; go manual.
fields.mistake: crawlers miss authenticated areas — replay with a session cookie.
fields.evidence: the URL list. **Old page content preserved:** the original notes had `hakrawler -url http://TARGET` and `katana -u http://TARGET -d 3`; the forms above add `-plain`/`-silent` for pipe-friendly output.

fields.lookFor: dangerous files, outdated components, missing headers, exposed directories.
fields.decision: every hit must be manually reproduced before it goes in the report.
fields.mistake: reporting Nikto output verbatim — it is noisy and produces false positives.
fields.evidence: only the confirmed findings. **Old page content preserved:** the original Nikto note also used `nikto -h TARGET -p 8080` for a non-standard port; that form is still correct.

blocks.title: Manual validation checklist
blocks.notes:
- **Parameters** — try a quote (`'`) and watch for SQL errors; try `../../` for traversal.
- **File upload** — extension filtering, content-type checks, upload directory reachable over HTTP.
- **Auth logic** — forced browsing, IDOR (change an object id), default credentials.
- **Verbose errors** — stack traces reveal paths, frameworks and sometimes credentials.
- **Known CMS plugins** — enumerate versions, match against public advisories.
> Only run the intrusive items above where the engagement allows it. On the exam, an unrequested destructive test can invalidate a machine.

blocks.title: Consider automated scanners carefully
blocks.notes: Automated web scanners (sqlmap with aggressive options, nuclei, wapiti) may be restricted by the current exam rules. **Confirm with the current official OffSec exam guide before relying on one.** Manual validation is always permitted and usually faster on a small app.

blocks.title: Get traffic into Burp

fields.lookFor: requests that differ from the browser's (hidden parameters, JSON bodies, custom headers).
fields.decision: an endpoint worth manipulating → Repeater. A parameter worth enumerating → Intruder (mind the rate).
fields.next: return to Step 14 with real requests.
fields.mistake: testing without Burp's proxy in scope, then losing the request that worked.
fields.evidence: export the request/response pair for the report.

blocks.notes:
1. Browser proxy → `127.0.0.1:8080` (or use FoxyProxy with a profile).
2. Install Burp's CA: browse to `http://burp/cert`, import into the browser trust store.
3. Set **Target → Scope** to the lab host so history stays readable.
4. `curl` requests can be replayed: copy as `curl` from Burp, or send a request to **Repeater** and edit it.

blocks.text: | Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `curl: (60) SSL certificate problem` | Self-signed cert | `-k` | | `curl: (7) Failed to connect` | Wrong port, or service bound to [localhost](http://localhost) | Re-check the port scan; pivot through the host | | Redirect loop | Cookie or host mismatch | Use the hostname from `Location`, not the IP | | 403 on every path | WAF or IP allow-list | Slow down, change User-Agent, check for vhosts | | 200 on everything | Catch-all/wildcard | Filter by size (`-fs`), not status | | Empty body but 200 | JS-rendered SPA | Read the bundle (Step 11) | | Site works with IP, breaks with hostname | Missing `/etc/hosts` entry | Add it | | `nikto` finds nothing | Wrong scheme/port | Try `-ssl`, and the exact port |
**Stop condition:** when headers, source, robots and one manual pass produce no lead, move to another service. Re-fuzzing the same wordlist is not new information.

items: `nmap -sCV -p<HTTP_PORT> --script http-title,http-headers`.
`whatweb -a 1` → `-a 3` if needed.
`curl -i -sS -L` — headers, redirects, cookies.
`robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml`, page source.
`openssl s_client... subjectAltName` — new hostnames.
`ffuf` vhost discovery → add names to `/etc/hosts`.
Auth: identify mechanism, capture a session.
JS: endpoints and hidden routes.
`nikto` for breadth, then manual validation.
Burp for anything stateful.
Directory brute force → the Directory & VHost page.
The header block per port (server, framework, cookies).
Certificate SAN list.
Every vhost/hostname you added to `/etc/hosts`.
The authenticated request/response pair.
Confirmed Nikto findings only, each with a manual reproduction.

WhatWeb: [https://github.com/urbanadventurer/WhatWeb](https://github.com/urbanadventurer/WhatWeb)
