pages.title: Exam Execution & Reporting — Proof, Timeline and Submission
pages.description: the exam is scored on **flags plus evidence**, not on shells. Build the workspace, capture proof in a form a grader accepts, and keep a timeline — before exam day, so it is habit rather than panic.

items: Three standalone machines (60 points) plus one Active Directory set of three machines (40 points), **23 hours 45 minutes**, then **24 hours** to upload the report.
AI chatbots and similar assistants are **prohibited** during the exam.
Scoring is scaled from **1 December 2026**; the current guide no longer restates a raw pass mark — **confirm with the current official guide**.
Full rules: **OSCP Exam Rules & Tool Restrictions**. No page here overrides the official guide.

fields.lookFor: four directories, created once, at the start.
fields.decision: every artefact goes into one of them — scans by host, loot by host, screenshots by sequence, notes by host.
fields.mistake: saving evidence to `~/Downloads` or `/tmp`. Files there get lost on reboot or collided between hosts.
fields.evidence: the directory listing.

fields.lookFor: a path you can reconstruct a week later.
fields.decision: host-first naming (`<IP>__`) sorts correctly and survives copy/paste into the report.
fields.mistake: `screenshot1.png`. Twenty of those and you cannot tell which host or which privilege level it proves.
fields.evidence: the naming scheme in use.

commands.code:
whoami; hostname; ip a; cat /etc/hostname
cat /root/local.txt
cat /root/proof.txt

fields.lookFor: the flag contents, plus hostname/IP visible **in the same terminal**.
fields.decision: `local.txt` proves user, `proof.txt` proves root — capture both at the moment you obtain them.
fields.mistake: capturing the flag, then closing the shell, then having no proof of **which** host it came from.
fields.evidence: one screen showing the command, the flag, and `ip a`/`hostname`.

commands.code:
whoami; hostname; ipconfig
type C:\Users\<USERNAME>\Desktop\local.txt
type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt

fields.lookFor: `nt authority\system` or the Administrator context, the hostname, the IPv4 address, and the flag.
fields.decision: Administrator vs SYSTEM matters for the write-up — state which account you used.
fields.mistake: running `type` in a different session from `whoami`. The grader must see them together.
fields.evidence: the combined output in one screenshot.

fields.lookFor: the correct file for the privilege level you reached.
fields.decision: `local.txt` without `proof.txt` means the box is half-done — do not move on and forget it.
fields.mistake: copying the flag into notes without a screenshot. Notes are supporting evidence; the screenshot is the proof.
fields.evidence: the file path and the flag value.

commands.code:
scrot -s ~/exam/screens/$(date +%H%M%S)_proof.png
# alternative, if scrot is unavailable: use the hypervisor/VM screenshot tool

fields.lookFor: a PNG that includes the flag **and** the host identity.
fields.decision: `scrot` is not installed on this host — install it on your own exam VM, or use the VM console's screenshot function. Test the chosen method **before** exam day.
fields.mistake: cropping the screenshot so the hostname/IP disappears. Never crop the terminal header.
fields.evidence: the PNG file itself, named with host and purpose.

blocks.title: The one-image rule

fields.lookFor: no ambiguity about which machine the flag belongs to.
fields.decision: you cannot prove host identity → the flag is worth nothing in a dispute. Recapture.
fields.mistake: proving root access with a screenshot of `id` only. That shows a privilege level, not a completed box.
fields.evidence: the paired images, sequentially numbered.

blocks.notes: A grader should be able to look at **one image** and see: the flag, the account, and the host. If a single terminal cannot show all three (e.g. a GUI-only path), take two consecutive screenshots and label them `<IP>_proof_a` and `<IP>_proof_b`.

fields.lookFor: a monotonic log of what you did and when.
fields.decision: useful when the report needs "initial access at …", and when you must explain a gap.
fields.next: append a one-line entry at each major milestone.
fields.mistake: writing the timeline at the end from memory. It will be wrong, and it reads like it.
fields.evidence: `~/exam/notes/timeline.txt`.

blocks.title: Per-machine notes

fields.lookFor: enough detail that you could redo the box from the notes alone.
fields.decision: if a step produced a credential or a shell, it belongs in the notes **and** in the final report.
fields.mistake: notes that record only the final command. The report needs the path, including failed branches that explain your choices.
fields.evidence: one note file per host.

blocks.notes: Use the **OSCP Machine Notes — Template** page for every host: IP, hostname, open ports, credentials found, exploitation path, privilege escalation, flags, and screenshot filenames.

blocks.title: Time budget

fields.lookFor: a box that has consumed its budget without a foothold.
fields.decision: park it, take the easy points elsewhere, come back with fresh eyes.
fields.next: move to the next target and log the switch in the timeline.
fields.mistake: sinking 8 hours into one machine while three others remain untouched.
fields.evidence: the budget vs actual, in the timeline.

blocks.notes: A workable split for 23h45m: roughly 12 hours for the three standalone machines, 6-7 hours for the AD set, and the remaining time for reporting and re-checks. Treat these as targets, not rules — the official guide is authoritative on timing.

fields.lookFor: a hash list you can re-verify before upload.
fields.decision: hashes differ after copying → the copy corrupted (rare); re-copy before submitting.
fields.next: keep the hash file with the report.
fields.mistake: hashing an empty glob (no files matched) and calling it verified. Check the file count first.
fields.evidence: the hash list and the matching files.

blocks.title: Revert a broken target

fields.lookFor: the documented revert control in the exam environment — not a guess at `vmrun` or a hypervisor CLI.
fields.decision: the box is unstable or credentials are bricked → revert, then redo only the steps needed to regain your position.
fields.next: re-capture proof if the revert lost it.
fields.mistake: reverting after you already captured the flag and losing the shell state — capture and hash proof **before** any revert.
fields.evidence: the timeline entry for the revert and the reason.

blocks.notes: If an exploit crashes a service or you lock yourself out, revert the machine to the **exam-provided snapshot** before re-attacking. Re-read the exam guide for the exact revert procedure and any scoring implications.

pages.title: Troubleshooting — Complete Command Reference
pages.description: when something "does not connect", find the layer that is broken in under two minutes — interface/route, DNS, TCP, HTTP, or the proxy in between — instead of re-running the exploit.

blocks.text: | Test | Layer | A healthy result | | --- | --- | --- | | `ip a`, `ip route`, `ping` | L3 | an address, a default route, replies | | `dig`, `getent hosts` | DNS | the expected IP | | `nc -nv IP PORT` | L4 | `succeeded` / `open` | | `ss -tlnp` | local stack | your listener bound | | `curl -v` | L7 | headers, status code | | `tcpdump` | ground truth | SYN, SYN-ACK, or nothing |
Work **down** the list. The first failing row is the problem.

blocks.title: Check the local stack and route

commands.code:
ip a; ip route; ping -c 3 <TARGET_IP>
ip route get <TARGET_IP>

fields.lookFor: an address on the correct interface, a default route, and ICMP replies.
fields.decision: no reply but the route exists → ICMP may be filtered; continue to Step 03 (TCP). Wrong interface/route → fix VPN/routing before anything else.
fields.mistake: treating a failed `ping` as "host down". Many exam targets drop ICMP while serving TCP perfectly.
fields.evidence: the `ip a`/`ip route` output and the ping result.

fields.lookFor: the intended resolver, the expected A record, and `getent` agreeing with `dig`.
fields.decision: `dig` works but an application fails → the app uses `/etc/hosts` or a different resolver. Add the entry explicitly.
fields.mistake: debugging DNS when you should use the IP. If the record is wrong, put the mapping in `/etc/hosts` and move on.
fields.evidence: the resolver config and the resolved address.

commands.code:
nc -nv <TARGET_IP> <TARGET_PORT>
# scriptable
nc -z -v <TARGET_IP> <TARGET_PORT> && echo OPEN || echo CLOSED

fields.lookFor: `succeeded` / `open`, or a banner.
fields.decision: open but the exploit fails → the service is there; the problem is protocol/credentials. Closed/timeout → firewall or wrong port.
fields.next: Step 04 (if you expect a listener) or Step 05 (HTTP).
fields.mistake: testing through proxychains when the tool uses UDP, or forgetting that `-z` sends no payload and some services log it.
fields.evidence: the probe result.

fields.lookFor: the port bound to `0.0.0.0` vs `127.0.0.1`.
fields.decision: bound to `127.0.0.1` → only local processes can reach it; tunnel in (Tunneling page). Not listening → the service is down.
fields.mistake: starting a listener on `127.0.0.1` and expecting a remote callback. Bind `0.0.0.0` or the correct interface.
fields.evidence: the `ss` line for the port.

commands.code:
curl -v http://<TARGET_IP>:<TARGET_PORT>/
curl -vk https://<TARGET_IP>:<TARGET_PORT>/
curl -v --resolve <DOMAIN>:<TARGET_PORT>:<TARGET_IP> https://<DOMAIN>:<TARGET_PORT>/

fields.lookFor: `Connected to …`, the request line, response headers, and the status code.
fields.decision: HTTP works but the browser/app does not → vhost or Host header. TLS handshake fails → `-k` or SNI (use `--resolve`).
fields.next: the HTTP or Directory & VHost page.
fields.mistake: reading only the body. `-v` shows the redirect, the auth challenge, and the exact header causing the failure.
fields.evidence: the `-v` transcript.

commands.code:
sudo tcpdump -i <INTERFACE> -nn -A port <TARGET_PORT>
sudo tcpdump -i <INTERFACE> -nn -w <OUTPUT_FILE> host <TARGET_IP>

fields.lookFor: whether packets leave, and whether anything returns.
fields.decision: SYN out, nothing back → filtered/routed wrong. SYN, RST → port closed. SYN, SYN-ACK, then RST → TLS/app mismatch. Nothing at all → wrong interface.
fields.next: fix the layer the capture proves is broken.
fields.mistake: capturing on `eth0` while the traffic uses `tun0`. Confirm with `ip route get <TARGET_IP>`.
fields.evidence: the pcap file, or the filtered output showing the handshake.

blocks.title: Read the failure correctly

fields.mistake: jumping to the exploit when the handshake already shows the port is closed. Read the four packets first.

blocks.notes:
| Capture / probe result | Meaning | Next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SYN sent, no reply | Filtered, or wrong route | `ip route get`, try the pivot |
| SYN → RST | Closed | Wrong port / service down |
| SYN → SYN-ACK → RST | App or TLS mismatch | `curl -v`, `-k`, SNI |
| Connection open, no data | Protocol mismatch | Try the right client |
| Works locally, fails remotely | Bound to 127.0.0.1 | Rebind / tunnel |
| Works from pivot, not Kali | Routing between Kali and pivot | Check the tunnel |

blocks.title: Verify the path through a proxy

commands.code:
proxychains4 -q curl -v http://<INTERNAL_IP>/
proxychains4 -q nc -nv <INTERNAL_IP> <TARGET_PORT>
nmap -Pn -sT -p <TARGET_PORT> <INTERNAL_IP>

fields.lookFor: responses that only appear when the proxy is in use.
fields.decision: `curl` fails but `nc` works → application issue, not routing. Both fail → the pivot cannot reach the target; test from the pivot itself.
fields.mistake: using `-sS` or ICMP through a SOCKS proxy. Use `-sT -Pn`.
fields.evidence: the proxied transcript.

blocks.title: Systematic checklist
blocks.notes:
1. `ip a` — am I on the right network?
2. `ip route get <TARGET_IP>` — which interface will it use?
3. `getent hosts` — does the name resolve to the IP I expect?
4. `nc -nv` — is the port actually open?
5. `ss -tlnp` — is my listener bound where I think?
6. `curl -v` — what does the application say?
7. `tcpdump` — what actually crosses the wire?
8. Only then revisit the exploit.
**Rule:** never change the exploit until one of these eight tests has failed. Guessing wastes more time than measuring.

blocks.text: | Symptom | Start at | Do **not** | | --- | --- | --- | | Nothing responds at all | Step 01 | Reinstall the tool | | Name does not resolve | Step 02 | Hard-code and forget the cause | | Port "closed" | Step 03 | Assume the host is down | | Callback never arrives | Step 04 | Regenerate the payload | | HTTP 400/404/redirect | Step 05 | Blame the exploit | | Works locally, fails remotely | Step 04 (bind address) | Add firewall rules blindly | | Only through a proxy | Step 08 | Use a SYN scan | | Everything looks fine | Step 06 (capture) | Keep retrying |

The layer that was actually broken, and the test that proved it.
Any routing or `/etc/hosts` change you made (so you can undo it).
The pcap if the failure was intermittent.
